summary: Section 2(1)(f) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 defines "adulterated article" to mean any of the articles of food which is adulterated only when it is insect infested. Section 2(i)(f), as amended by the Eastern Book Company Limited (Amendment) Act, 1978, provides that the word "otherwise" in sub clause (f) with slight consequent rearrangement and parenthesis would read like this: "if the article is unfit for human consumption on account of (a) its consisting wholly or in part of any filthy, putrid, disgusting, rotten, decomposed or diseased animal or vegetable substance or being insectinfested, (b) or on account, of any other cause". The Food Inspector, P.W. 4, took a sample of Lalacheroo Mal 's living meal worms. There was no other evidence in support of the case of the prosecution that the lal mirchi powder was adulterated and he accordingly acquitted the respondent. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant Corporation that (i) the Food Inspector had not established by any satisfactory evidence the requirement of section 2(l)(f). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The words "or is otherwise unfit for life" are disjunctive of the rest of the words preceding them. The presumption may not be conclusive in all cases irrespective of the character of the article, and the nature and extent of the vice afflicting it. This is particularly so where an article is found to be "insect infest infested". In Municipal Corporation of Delhi vs Kacheroo Chand Bhatia (1980) 1 S.C.R. 1, this Court held that if for an article of food, no(1) standard of quality or purity has been prescribed or no limits have been prescribed for the validity or its constituents, then sub clause 2 will not apply and that the Public Analyst is not competent to say as to what extent of insect, infestation would make the article 'adulterised ' for human ' consumption. [473F G] (2) The High Court was clearly wrong in holding that the report of the Public analyst was vague, inadequate and deficient and in the absence of clear proof of the sample being unfit for any human consumption. Therefore, no interference is called for with the judgment of acquittal passed by the trying Magistrate and upheld by the High Court. [474G H] Dhanraj 's case (supra) referred to.

The appellant was prosecuted under section 7 of the Essential Commodities Act for violation of cl. 3(2) of the order dated May 28, 1966 passed by the Magistrate, First Class and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for six months. On appeal, the Sessions Judge acquitted the appellant on the ground that the lease deeds were not registered and were not admissible in evidence under section 49 of the Registration Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the presumption under para. 3 (2) could not be drawn against him because the presumption in his case cannot be drawn. HELD : (i) The presumption under paragraph 3(1) couldnot be drawn from proof of storage only. It is obvious that sub paragraph speaks of storage for sale as a dealer although the words "as a dealer" are not there, because storage has reference to business as a dealers and that is the essence of the Order. The fiction in the second sub paragraph must be carried to its logical conclusion. In the present case, the appellant produced a number of lease deeds in which leases of various parcels of land were shown to have been granted to him. He also produced receipts of payment of lease money and he cited witnesses who deposed on oath that he and his brother cultivated 80 90 bighas of land. No doubt, the lease deed is not registered but for the purpose of a criminal prosecution, it has to be proved that they are genuine or not and whether an inference of innocence can be based upon them. [90 F G] Manipur Administration vs M. Nila Chandra Singh, ; , referred to. (ii)The presumption under Para. 3)(2) cannot be draw against the appellant because there is nothing in the case to show that the lands about which the witnesses spoke orally were held by him for purposes of cultivation. If that be so, then he is an agriculturist and it is easy to see that the evidence which wasbrought for ward of witnesses deposing orally was not concocted to set up a false defence. Indeed no adequate reasons were given for rejecting the testimony of one witness on the question whether he was an agriculturist or not.

The defendant was a monthly tenant in respect of the suit land. He continued to be a monthly tenancy from month to month under section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act, and continued as such for more than 12 years. The plaintiff instituted a suit against the defendant for ejectment of a lessee on the ground that he had acquired permanent rights in the land under a lease from month 'to month under the provisions of section 106 of the Indian Evidence Act. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal, the High Court confirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the defendant (i) that by reason of the payment and acceptance of rent there were two tenancies for one year each for two successive years; and (ii) that in view of the provisions contained in section 116 Transfer of property Act, there could be no question of a monthly lease being brought into existence under the Transfer Of Property Act. HELD : (i)(a) It is well settled that the mode in which a rent is expressed to be payable affords a presumption that the tenancy is of a character corresponding there to. But the difficulty in applying this rule to the present case arises from the fact that a tenancy from year to month or reserving a yearly rent can be made only by registered instrument, as laid down in section 107 of the Act. [280 D F] (b) It was not correct to say that a lease for one years certain might fairly be inferred from the payment of annual rent and a stipulation like that would not come within the mischief of section 107 Of the Transfer 'of Property Act because it is quite another thing to substitute a new agreement for the parties which is palpably contradicted by the admit ted facts of the case. It would be pertinent to point out in tiffs connection with the payment made by the Receiver, that the rent was intended to be for a period exceeding one year but as the intention was not expressed in the proper legal form, it could not be given effect to. [281 F H] (ii)(a).

Section 137 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 provides that where a person makes an application to the Commissioner in the prescribed form for any information relating to any assessee in respect of any assessment made either under this Act or the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, on or after April 1, 1964, the Commissioner may, if he is satisfied that it is in the public interest so to do, furnish or cause to be furnished such information asked for. Sub section (1) of Section 138 provides that notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, no court shall save as provided in this Act, be entitled to require any public servant to produce before it any such return, accounts, documents or record or any part of any such record, or to give evidence before it in respect thereof. Section 138(1)(b) provides that a person making an application under the Income tax law to the Commis sioner shall be treated as confidential and notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, no Court shall save with any court of law. Section 137(1) empowers the Board or any other income tax authority specified by it by a general or special order in that behalf to furnish or causes to be furnishing the information asked by an assessee or a third party after April l, 1964 in respect Of the assessment years 1964 65 onwards. The proviso to this sub section states that where the documents, records, etc. were filed before the income tax authorities after April I, 1964 for the said assessment years taking place under the Indian Incometax Act, the IncomeTax Officer may, notwithstanding anything in any law for time being In force, make an order requiring the production of such documents, record, etc., as are found relevant to a case pending before him. The High Court took the view that the omission of section 137 did not make any difference and that the ban on the courts as contained in section 138(l)(b), had no relationship to the power of the court to summon the production. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1.

One Mammotty was married to Seinaba and he made a gift of his properties including immovable property in favour of Seinba. He also executed a will whereby he bequeathed his properties to Seinsi and his two sisters. The mother died on May 3, 1946, without leaving any issue. She then filed a suit for partition and possession of the property which was decreed by the trial court and confirmed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) when the donor and donee reside together an overt act only is necessary and this rule applies between husband and wife; and (2) in any view of the matter when a husband makes a gift to a minor, he must depart from it and the donee must enter upon possession. HELD : (i) It was not correct to say that there was a complete intention to divest ownership on the part of Mammottty and to transfer the property to the donee. If the property is with the donor he must follow his own rules and must be based on justice, equity and good conscience and should not be hare belonging to him to show his ownership and possession. Exceptions to these strict rules which are well recognised are gifts by the wife to the husband and by the father to his minor child (Macnaghten page 51) where there is gift to the minor who has no guardian of the properties in existence. In such cases the benefit to the minors and the completion of the gift for his benefit is the sole consideration. [557 D E] (ii) The rule about possession is relaxed in certain circumstances by providing that a donor must not leave behind even a straw belonging to himself to show the ownership and posses sion of the land or any zamindari estate in existence, and not from any supposed authority; and this necessity cannot exist whilst the father is present. [558 E F] (iii) The gift in the present case was a valid gift. Mammutty was living at the time of the gifted property in the house of his mother in law and was probably a very sick person though not in marzulmaut. His minor wife who had attained discretion was capable under Muhammadan Law to accept the gift, was living in her own house and in her care where the husband was also residing.

The Madras Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951 was enacted to provide for the better administration and governance of Hindu Religious and charitable institutions and endowments in the State of Madras. Section 76(1) provides that the trustee of every religious institution shall keep regular accounts of all receipts and disbursements. The Commissioner of Hindu religious and charitable Endowments issued a notice under section 76(2) calling upon the respondent to pay the arrears of contributions and audit fee under the Commissioner 's demand notice dated June 25, 1957. The respondents challenged the validity of the demand on the ground that no rules had been framed under section 100 of the Act and therefore the demand was premature. The High Court held that sections 21, 30(2), 31, 55, 56 and 63 of the Madras Hindu Religious & Charitable Endowments (Amendment) Act, 1954 were ultra vires the State Legislature. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (1) that section 76 (1), providing for imposing liability for payment of contribution which was of the nature of a tax does not cease to be of that character merely because there is an element of compulsion or coerciveness present in it, nor is it a postulate of a fee that it must have direct relation to the levy and the expenses incurred for rendering the service are met out of the amounts collected there being a reasonable relation between the levy, and the expenditure incurred for maintaining the service. HELD: (i) Section 76 (2) provides for imposing a flat rate of audit fee on the religious institutions governed by the provisions of the Tamil Nadu Act 19 of 1951. The power to make rules was not restricted nor were the rules framed by the Government rendered invalid. [923 B C] (ii) It is true that ordinarily a fee is uniform and no account is taken of the varying abilities of different recipients. But absence of uniformity is not a criterion on which alone it can be said that it is of the kind of tax. A fee being a levy in consideration of rendering service of a particular type, co relation between its expenditure by the Govern ment and the levy must undoubtedly exist, but a levy will not be regarded as a tax merely because of the absence of any uniformity in its incidence or because of compulsion in the collection thereof, nor because some of the contri butories do not obtain the same degree of service as others may. [ 923 C D] (iii) The High court erred in holding that appropriate rules were not in existence at the time when the demand for audit fee was made and on that account the demand could not be sustained merely because it turns out that the amount demanded is not precisely equivalent to the cost actually incurred for auditing the accounts.

The appellant alleged that the notice was issued in accordance with the procedure prescribed under section 17 of the , to show cause against his alleged liability to be punished under section 15. A preliminary objection was raised by the respondents that no appeal lies to this Court under section 19 of the Act from an order issuing notice as nothing yet has been decided by the High Court. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the proceeding is not barred under section 20 of the . Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: An order merely initiating the proceeding without anything further, does not decide anything against the alleged contemner and cannot be appealed against as a matter of right from any order or decision of a bench of the High court if the order has been made in the exercise of its jurisdiction to punish for contempt. No appeal can lie as a matters of right under section19. In a given case special leave may be granted under article 136 of the Constitution from an Order initiating the proceedings. But that is entirely a different matter. What is deciding in this case is whether the person proceeded against has committed contempt of the Court or not. The matter has to be decided either finally or, may be even at an earlier stage an order is made, which does decide a contention raised before the High Courts affecting the right of the party aggrieved. Mere initiation of a proceeding for contempt by the issuance of the notice on the prima facie view that the case is a fit one for drawing up the proceeding does not deciding any question. This Court, therefore, cannot be asked in such an appeal to decide whether the persons proceeded against have committed contempt or not [512 G H] Baradakanta Mishra vs Orissa High Court, ; , referred to.

The appellant was prosecuted along with another under section 6(1 A) of the , for possessing a wireless transmitter in contravention of the provisions of section 3 of the Indian Telegraphy (Amendment) Act, 1949. The trial Magistrate convicted him and sentenced him to six months rigorous imprisonment. On appeal, the High Court confirmed both the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that section 6 (1 A), as amended by the Amending Act of 1949, had no application to a case of a later amending Act inserting new provisions in an earlier Act. HELD : Section 4 of the Repealing and Amending Act, 1952, is designed to provide for a different situation, namely, the repeal of an earlier enactment which has been applied, incorporated or referred to in a later Act. Under hat section the repeal by this Act of any enactment shall not affect any other enactment in which the repealed enactment has been applies, incorporated, or referred, to. [760 B C] In the present case, the insertion of section 6 A was not a textual amendment but a substantial one. The object of the repealing and amending Act of 1952 was only to strike out the unnecessary Acts and excise dead matter from the statute book in order to lighten the burden of ever increasing spate of legislation and to remove confusion from the public mind. [764 C D] State of Punjab vs M/s. Karnail Kaur, ; , referred to. There is no foundation for this argument that section 4 of Act XVII of 1933 was intended to provide a different situations, namely the repeal or amendment of an existing law by a third does not affect the continuance of the amendment made by the enactment so repealed. The earlier Act cannot incorporate the later Act but can only be amended by it.

The appellant, who was the managing Shebait of the deities from 1926 to 1930, instituted a suit for recovery of moneys due in respect of the Hatchita and the promissory notes executed by her in favour of one Nanitosh Chakraborty. The suit was decreed on the basis of a compromise dated 23rd July, 1933, and two consent decrees were passed one for a sum of Rs. 5,068 and the other for Rs. 2,200. In execution of these decrees the properties mentioned in Schedule Ka were attached and put up to sale and they were purchased ostensibly by the appellant on the strength of an agreement dated 23th July, 1932, which was entered into between the appellant and Nanitta Nath Roy, a managing Shebaita of the debutter estate. The appellant contended that the properties described in Schedules Ka and Kha were not liable to be partitioned under section 36(2)(c) of the Bengal Money Lenders Act, 1934, as they had been purchased ostensibly for the purpose of substituting the method of accounting sanctioned by the Act for the calculations upon which the original decree was passed. Held, that the appellant was entitled to a declaration that the property in question was his benamidar for another person in respect Of the decree and not the one in whose favour the original sale deed was executed. The object of restoring possession of the properties sold in execution of the decree to the judgment debtor is to enable the latter to pay off the decretal dues, thus ascertained by instalments. Such an enquiry as to whether the ostensible purchaser at the execution sale, or the person who purports to have acquired an interest therein under a subsequent transfer from the decreeholder purchaser, has bonafide acquired such rights within the meaning of clause (b) of section 36 (2). Renula vs Manmatha, 72 I.A. 156, referred to.

The respondent obtained a decree against the appellant in respect of certain transactions in gold and silver effected by the appellant. The appellant filed an application before the City Civil Court under O. XXI, r. 16 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for execution of the decree passed by the City civil court in favour of the respondent on the ground that the respondent had not taken steps under 0. XXI. r.16 of the C.P.C. to get themselves substituted as plaintiffs in the place and stead of Habib & Sons, the appellant was not entitled to apply for execution. The City Civil Judge dismissed the application holding that the appellant could not apply under O, XXI, rule 16 of C. P.C., because (i) the decree had been transferred or agreed to be transferred by assignment in writing within the meaning of Order XXI, Rule 16; and (ii) as soon as the decree was passed, the respondent company became the transferees of the appellant 's decree. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that (i). under O., XXI, R. 16(old section 232 of the Civil Procedure Code, execution proceedings could be taken and application for execution was maintainable by a suit for specific performance as contemplated by Order XXI Rule 16 of 'the Code of civil procedure; (ii). The respondent could not claim to come under O XXI, rr. 16 and 17 of the code of Civil procedure because (a) the appellant had in his application for executing the decree in the present case filed before the city Civil Court not mentioned any of these particulars but had only stated that the court should declare them the assignees of the suit as the decretal debt along with other debts were transferred by the deed of assignment dated the 7th February, 1949; (b) the respondent was entitled to execute the decree on the basis of O. 21, r., 16 of 0. 16, which enables him to obtain the leave of the court to continue the suit; and, (c) the High Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the application for the execution of a decree under Order XXI. Rule 16(2)(j). HELD: (i ) The respondent cannot claim to be a transferee of the judgment debtor by assignment of a debt which was subsequently obtained by Habib & sons by an assignment in the writing executed before the decree came into existence and that while a transfer of or an agreement to transfer a decree that may be passed in future may entitle the intending transferee to claim the beneficial interest in the decree after it is passed, such equitable transfer does not render the transferee a transferee. [1423 D E] (ii)(a) The words "decree holder" must be construed as meaning decree holder in fact and not as including a party who in equity may afterwards become entitled to the rights of the actual decree holder and that the language of O, 21, R., 16 is plain and unambiguous. [ 1424 F G] (b)(i) In the instant case the respondent could only make an application for leave under Order 21, rule 11 of C P. C. to execute it in the same manner and subject to the same conditions as if the application were made by the transferor in writing or by operation of law within the scope of O., 21, rr., 16(1) and 16(3). [1424 F H] (2)(a)(ii) The respondent was not a transferee for the enforcement of any decree passed against him after it had been passed. [1525 B C] (3)(b)(iii) If the respondents could not avail themselves of O '21, r, 16(i), they would be entitled to obtain leave of Court under 0 21, Rule 11(2) (j). [1526 F G]. Bhagwant Balajirao & Ors. vs Rajaram Sajnaji & Ors., I.L.R. , approved.

The respondent, a manufacturer of steel doors, windows and other goods, entered into an agreement with the Executive Engineer, Ajmer Central Division, for providing and fixing the windows to the appellant 's factory. The contract provided that the fittings and service were to be performed by plain glass or ground glass as may be decided by the Engineer in Charge, and were to he fitted with rawlanding materials in cut stone work. On April 20, 1957, the respondent submitted its tender for providing the doors and windows in a specified building. The appellant, however, did not accept it and carried out the contract. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court of Rajasthan challenging the contract on the ground that the contract was one of sale of goods and the respondent had with a view to promote sales of goods manufactured by it "voluntarily offered to fit" the goods and had made no separate charge for that service, and that the price of the supplied but not the charge for service was taxable. The High Court held that the appellant was liable to pay sales tax on the value of materials supplied in carrying out the contracts. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (1) that the respondent carried on the business of fabricating and selling window and door leaves and sashes etc., and entered into a contract for "sale of windows" and to promote sale of its manufactured goods, undertaken to fix the windows without demanding any charge for such service; and (2) that in undertaking to install or fix these structures or articles, the sellers do not enter into a works contract merely because they undertake to install and fix them to make them fit for immediate service. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) The object of the respondent was to enter into "a works contract". That clearly appears from the terms of the tender and its acceptance. The windows were to have been fabricated according to specifications with glass plain or ground as decided by Engineer in charge, and are to be "fixed" within six months from the date of its acceptance "to the building with raw material". [516 B C] (ii) It was only upon the "fixing" of the window leaves and when the window left had become a part of the building construction that the property in the goods passed under the contract, and not before. The test in each case is whether the object of a party sought to be taxed is that the chattel as chattel passes to the other party and the services rendered in connection with the installation are under a separate contract or are incidental to the execution of the contract of sale. In the present case, the specifications of the windows were set out in the contract and the primary undertaking of the respond ent was not merely to supply the windows but to "fix" the windows. The service is not rendered under a different contract nor is the service shown to be rendered customarily or normally as incidental to sale by the person who supplies window leaves. The "fixation" of windows in the manner stipulated required special technical skill. If the windows are not properly "fixed", the contract would not be complete, and the Respondent could not claim the amount agreed to be paid to it. [517 C D] (iii) It is only upon a "fixed" of special skill and labour by the experienced engineers and mechanics of the assessees that the materials in the construction of a building become the property of the other parties, to the contract only on the theory of accretion. In The State of Madras vs Gannon Dunkerley & Co., (Madras) Ltd., ; , it was held that where there is a contract to "Fixing" certain articles made by a manufacturer the contract must be deemed one for sale and not of service.

The prosecution case was that on November 8, 1967 Shankerlal representing himself to be a broker of foreign machinery parts went to Ram Avtar and told him that he (Shanker Lal) could arrange for a transaction of sale of foreign goods which would result in good profit to the complainant. The complainant agreed to purchase 200 pieces of the washer plates at the rate of Rs. 38/ per piece. Formal order, it was then agreed, would be sent through Shankar Lal. On November 16, 1967 Shankarlal handed over the formal order to Ram Av Kumar and Raj Kumar Agarwalla and Shankar Lal took one Saheb Jaman Khan along with him to Ram Awana and introduced Saheb Jamyan Khan as agent of M/s. Ashoke Trading Corporation of Indore. The prosecution case against the accused was that he had agreed to the proposal and wanted to see the seller of the foreign goods in question. On the following day, Shankar Lal brought one Saheb jaman Khan alongwith him to the shop of Ram Avtar. A day after that day, Shankerlal and Rajkumar Agarwalla came to the appellant 's shop and told them that he was an agent of Shri Hanuman Agency and would supply the foreign good known as washer plate. Pandey showed Ram Avtar the samples of those wereher plates. One of those samples was kept by Ram Avtar in a taxi and demanded the price of Rs 38/per piece. The accused were thereafter arrested by the police on November 15, 1967. The case against him was quashed by the High Court on the ground that so far as Raj Kumar Agawalla was concerned, no case had been made out against him. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant State that there was no cogent ground for interference with the judgment of the High court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) There is no infirmity in the judgment as might induce us to interfere. The report which was lodged by Ram Manohar Lal in the very nature of things made no mention of the name of Raj Kumar Aggarwala respondent because it is the case of the prosecution itself that Raj Kumar appeared on the scene only subsequent to the lodging of the report. The part which is attributed to Raj Kumar is that he has a party to any conspiracy to defraud or cheat Ram Avtar, and that Raj Kamal Singh and Saheb Jamn Khan were also told that this transaction would fetch him a profit of Rs 3200/ . On November 15 1967, the proceedings were set in motion against the appellant after his suspicion had been aroused. Therefore, there is no cogent reason for interference. [280 D E] (2) The report was lodged on November 16. 1967 and the accused were discharged.

The petitioner, a resident of Sultanbattery area in the State of Kerala and describing himself as a commuter of the Indian Railways, has alleged violation of fundamental rights guaranteed under Articles 19 and 21 of the Constitution. It was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the Railways had violated the fundamental right guaranteed under Article 19(1)(g) of the Consti tution of India Act, 1890 to provide for such level crossings at their cost in view of the accepted position that at a level crossing the right of way, crossings could be undertaken. Dismissing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The Railways are a public utility service run on monopoly basis. Since it is a public interest litigation and the petitioner has attempted to voice the grievances of the community availing of the services of Indian Railways there is no justification to run it merely as a commercial venture with a view to making profits. [723F] 2. It is this class of passengers which is a menace to the system. Stringent laws should be made and strictly enforced to free the Railways from this deep rooted evil. Security both to the travelling public as also to the non travelling citizens must be provided and this means that accidents have to be avoided, attack on the persons of the passengers and prying on their property has to stop. Scientific improvements made in other countries and suitable to the systems in our country must be briskly adopted. The obligations cast by the Railways Act and the Rules under it must be complied with. It does not fall for consideration here if a monopoly based public utility should ever be a commercial activity geared to support the general revenue of the State but there is not an iota of doubt that the guarantees provided in Part III of the Constitu tion are fundamental and it is the paramount obligation of the state to ensure availability of situations, circumstances and environments in which every citizen can effectively exercise and enjoy those rights.

Section 13 of the Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagirs Abolition) Act, 1953 provides that any jagirdar entitled to compensation under section 11 or 12 shall, on or before the 31st day of July 1958 apply in writing to the Collector for determining the amount of compensation payable to him under the said section. Section 14(1) provides that every award made under section 13 or 14 shall be in the form prescribed in section 26 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 and the provisions of sections 17 and 19 of the said Act shall, so far as may be, apply to the making of such award. The appellants filed applications for restoration before the Tribunal on May 6, 1961. The Tribunal rejected these applications holding that they were barred under article 168 of the Limitation Act read with Regulation 55 and 041, rr. 17 and 18 of the Civil Procedure Code. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) Section 14 of the Mysore Merged Territory and Areas(Jagirs ' Abolition)Act, 1953 deals with the practice and procedure to be followed by the Gujarat Revenue Tribunal in case of non appearance of parties and to record its decision regarding the merits of the appeal. If an appeal is dismissed for want of prosecution it cannot be said that the Tribunal has decided the appeal on merits even though there is default on the part of the appellant to appear in the appeal; (ii) in Regulation 19(1), it is open to the Tribunal to dismiss an appeal for non prosecution in a case where the appellant does not appear either in person or through his agent or lawyer. It is also open to him to hear the respondent to the appeal and decide it on merits, after hearing the respondent or his agent, or lawyer; (iii) The Tribunal committed an error of law in dismissing the applications of restoration made by the appellants in all the four appeals.

The plaintiff 's case was that Telibandha village was dedicated to the temple of Shri Ramsaran temple and that he had committed several breaches of trust by transferring trust properties and appropriating its proceeds and finally by his express repudiation of this trust, the defendant had committed breach of trust. The trial court held that a valid trust had been created in favour of the temple and it was not satisfied that the dedication had been made by Dinanath Sao to the deity in the temple. On appeal, the High Court set aside the decree of the trial court and ordered the suit to be dismissed without going into other issues as regards the character of the property or whether the defendant bad committed breaches of the trust. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the use of the words "from the profits and income" in section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, showed that only a portion of the income was intended to be used and that there was no absolute dedication of the village for the temple; and (ii) even assuming it was open to the defendant to raise this point now, it had to be decided on the basis that the mere use of word "Malik" so clearly showed an intention to give an absolute and full ownership. HELD : (i)(a) The High Court 's order based on a construction of paragraph 2 of the Panch Faisla does not in any way affect the force or validity of the absolute nature of the dedication. The fact that the suit is stated to be decreed as compromised and the compromise appears to have been in accordance with Mr. Bagchi 's award gave the property to the members of the family with only a charge on it for the expenses of the Temple and did not make an absolute dedication in respect of the properties. [434 B C] (b) The fact, therefore, that Ramsaryan Lal used to credit the income from Teli Dasi to the Gharu Khata which was maintained for the general expenses of his family or that he made certain alienations of the said property cannot change the absolute dedication into a partial dedication. It may well be that Ramsalan Lal was himself led by the terms of the Bagchi award into thinking that the property belonged to the family and as owners had full right to make a valid dedication to the estate, the dedication as made in Para. 2 of this Panch Faishla was merely a presumption which can well be displaced by what follows in the same document as regards other co sharers between whom the partition was being made. [427 B C; 428 D E] (c) The mere fact that there is not a single word in Bagchi"s award to indicate, even remotely, that in his opinion, the award suffered from any infirmity. On the contrary, it is clear that the document (the Panch Faisala Award of 1896) clearly and unambiguously shows an intention not to make Ramsarans the absolute owner of the land but give him possession and management of the same for the benefit of Shri Ramchandra Swamy temple. [ 428 C D] (d) The document (exhibit P. 1) of 1897 clearly and unequivocally shows anabsolute dedication of a village to Shri Ramchandra Swami Temple, and it is not correct to say that these words as used in the original necessarily mean "from" the profits or income of Teligana". [427 D E].

The appellants were the President of a High Court and Chairman, Action Committee of the High Court described as contemner No. 2 was actively associated with the passing of the resolution which contained disparaging remarks about the Chief Justice and since he also issued that resolution for publication in newspapers, he was guilty of contempt of court. The High Court discharged the notices. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that they were guilty of contumacious conduct and had committed contempt of Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) It is true that the High Courts referred to the contumacious act of the appel lants but the High court did not wish to proceed against the appellants. [ 602D E] (3) In view of the fact that the notices were discharged, the appeal is disposed of with the aforesaid directions. The respondents Nos. 1 to 4 and their eldest brother filed an application under section 14 of the , before the Sub Judge, Hooghly for a direction on the arbitrator to file the award in the Court in Misc. Case No. 74 of 1977. The Sub Judge fixed the hearing of the arbitrators ' application to return the award to enable them to present the same before the sub Registrar for registration. On 26th July, 1978 the arbitrators made an application before the Subordinate Judge praying for a direc tion on the Arbitrator to file it in the court in Misc Case No 74 of1977. The High Court quashed the registration under Article 227 of the Constitution holding that during the subsistence of the interim injunction order on the arbitrators to maintain status quo till the disposal of Misc. case No.74 of 1977 initiated by the appellant No. 1, there was subsisting injunction preventing the arbitrators from taking any steps. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal and setting aside the order of the High Court, this Court, HELD: (1) An award affecting immovable properties as in the instant case should be registered. It is therefore, not necessary to discuss in detail the ratio of A the decision of this Court in Nityananda M. Joshi & Ors. vs Life Insurance Corporation of India and others; , which has been referred to by the Full Bench of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in M. Venkataratnam vs M. Chelamayya, A.I.R. 1967 Andhra Pradesh In the aforesaid view of the matter the judgment and order of this court cannot be sustained and are set aside. [123G H; 124A B] (2) An act of the Court shall prejudice no man. The law itself and the administration of it, said Sir W. Scott, with reference to an alleged infraction of the revenue laws must yield to that to which everything must bend, to necessity; the law, in its most positive and peremptory injunctions, is understood to disclaim, as it does in its general aphorisms, all intention of compelling impossibilities, and the administra tion of law must adopt that general exception in the consideration of all particular cases. In this case admittedly during the period from 26th of July 1978 to 20th December, 1982 there was a subsisting injunction restraining the arbitrators for taking any action.

Section 15 of the Bombay Hotel and Lodging Houses Rates Control Act, 1947 (Bom. 57 Of 1947) provides that notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in any law for the time being in force, a tenant may sublet any portion of his premises to a sub tenant, provided he is forthwith intimates in writing to his landlord (a) that the tenant has, since the coming into operation of this Act, sub let the whole or part of the premises or assigned or transferred in any other manner his interest therein; and (b) that he has not sublet the whole of the said premises or assign or transfer in any way his interest thereunder. Section 15 of that Act is based on public policy and it has been held by this Court in P. D. Aswani vs Kavashah Dinshah Mulla, ; , that if public policy demands it even an equal participant in the mischief of a provision which cannot be condoned by any conduct or agreement of parties, there can be no waiver of the statutory provisions of section 15 and section 23 of the Contract Act is not applicable to contracts also as they are personal rights. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that section 15 of Bombay Hotel & Lodging Houses (Control) Act,1947 which provides for the protection of private rights of the landlord and unless there is in the Act itself any provision to the same effect, such rights as far as they were personal rights may be parted with or renounced by the landlord. Held: (i) The provisions of sections 15(1)(e), 15(2) and 15(3) of Bombay Rents, Hotel Rates and Lodging House Rates Control (Control ) Act, 1946, are not inconsistent with section 15(4) of the Act which provides a remedy for the enforcement of private right by way of restitution though not on the contract. The provisions in sections 15 and 16 of the Indian Contract Act do not apply to contracts made in contravention of the express provision of that section. P.D. Aswan vs Kavasshah, A.I.R. 1943 P.C. 147, referred to. (ii)Section 15 is based upon public policy. It has been laid down by this court that if a party to an illegality appears, whether from the evidence given by one side or the other, the disclosure is fatal to the case. In such a case, it would be for the benefit of the parties to the difference between the contract and the written contract. If there is any inconsistency between the two sections of the Transfer of Property Act and section 15, it will be unenforceable if it infringes on the rights of others or would be against public policy or morals.

The appellant was a candidate for admission to the M.B.B./B.S. Course in the month of March, 1990 whereat the marks awarded by the examiners were found tampered with and the result declared on June 30, 1990. The results were published on June 31, 1990 and the formalities of valuation by the examiner of the answer sheets in each subject were completed on June 29, 1990, and the final result was declared on July 30,1990. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court against non declaration of the results and the High court directed the State Board to take expeditious action to declare the results of the examination within the specified time. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the Standing Committee of the concerned Divisional Board had power under the Act and Regulations to enquire into the use of unfair means at the final examina tion conducted by the Board, and therefore, the impugned notification was without authority of law. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the Standing Commit tee did not have any power to take disciplinary action against the examiners; (ii) the standing committee did not record any reason in support of its conclusion that the examinees or the parents or guardians were parties to the fabrication and the fabrication was done at their behest; (iii) there was no need for examining the witnesses on behalf the Board; and (iv) the procedure adopted by the Divisional Board was without jurisdiction. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The examination of the examiners is an integral part of while exercising the powers under Article 226 or article 136 of the Constitution, by the High Courts or of this Court. [790B] 1.2 In the instant case, the Standing Committees of the Divisional Boards had no power to interfere with the findings and to quash the impugned notifications.

The appellants were charged under section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code for criminal conspiracy to cause the offence of criminal misconduct punishable under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The trial court found them guilty and sentenced them to three months ' rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 5,000. On appeal the High Court reduced the sentence on the ground that section 5 (2) Of the Prevention Of Corruption Act was not applicable to the facts. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the offence as defined in clause (d) of cl. (d), does not come with in the meaning of bribery, and that even if it be held that the public servant adopted corrupt or illegal means and thereby obtained for himself or for any other person any valuable thing without consideration or for a consideration which he knows to be inadequate from any person whom he knew to have been, or to be likely to be concerned in any proceeding or business transacted or about to be transacted by him, or having any connection with the official functions of himself or of any public servant to whom he is subordinate or from any other persons who may be interested in or related to the person so concerned, or (c) if he dishonestly or fraudulently misappropriates or otherwise converts for his own use any property entrusted to him or under his control as a public servant or allows any other public servant in any way satisfactorily account, of pecuniary resources or property disproportionate to his known sources of income may be proved and on such proof the Court shall presume, unless the contrary is proved, that the accused person was guilty of criminal negligence in the discharge of his official duty and his conviction therefor shall not be invalid by reason only that it is based solely on such presumption. Held, further, that a speedy disposal of corruption cases by special courts, the benefit of in vestigation by higher police authorities are some of the provisions intended for the protection of public servants prosecuted under the Act while they are subjected to the same process as punishment and the application of the presumption referred to in sub section (3) of section 5 of the Act is not excluded.

The appellant Bank filed a suit for recovery of Rs. 76,368.04P on the ground that it had agreed to grant cash credit facility to deceased principal debtor on the security of goods by way of pledge and that since the goods were to be kept in the godown in the compound of Vijay Oil Mills Pvt. Ltd., the surety was not discharged from his liability under the guarantee. The trial court found that there was negligence on the part of the Bank with regard to safe custody of the pledged goods, but as the contract of guarantee entered into by the surety with the Bank was independent of the pledge of goods given by the principal debtor at one sitting on September 16, 1957, the surety would not be discharged from its liability under that guarantee. On appeal by the appellant, the High Court held that the surety had agreed and had in fact pledged 5,000 tins of oil tins with the bank as security for the advance and therefore the surety could not be absolved from his obligation under the guarantees. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant Bank that (i) the Bank had offered two securities, one the pledge and the other the personal guarantee of the surety; (ii) in view of clauses 5, 7 and 13 of the letter of guarantee dated February 14, 1961, even if it is found as a fact that negligence of the creditor bank was responsible for the loss of security of pledged goods yet the surety will not be relieved from his obligations undertaken under the letter dated February 15, 1961; (iii) in any event, if the creditor lost or without the consent of the sureties, part of security offered by the Principal debtor would have satisfied the Bank 's entire claim. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellant was the plaintiff and its suit was decreed by the trial court, i.e., the Court of first instance and this decree has been reversed by the High court in exercise of its appellate jurisdiction.

Held, that the appellant was not entitled to claim as of right that he had a share in the "patelki inam" lands as a member of the patel 's family, irrespective of whether he performs the service or not. Section 3 of the Patels and Patwaris (Abolition) Act, 1948, provides that the emoluments appertaining to the office of patel or patwari shall be enjoyed solely by the person for the time being holding the office; even a substitute shall receive the whole of the emoluments appurtenant to the post, unless the Deputy Commissioner otherwise directs, and if there are two or more patels in a village, the Deputy commissioner may direct that each patel shall hold office in turn by rotation for a term of not less than 10 years. The appellant was entitled to his share in "poli inam" as an undivided brother of Amritrao, Patel. He claimed that under section 3 of that Act he was entitled only to his half share in 'patelka inam ' lands and that the grant was made by the jagirdar of village Nawabag and not by the sovereign authority and neither the Inam Rules nor the provisions thereof applied to him. Held, that on a proper construction of sections 3 and 9 of the Act it is clear that there is nothing in them on the basis of which the appellant can claim as Of right that be has a share therein as a members of the village. The grant was not a service grant and no question of title by adverse possession arose against Government, even though the lands were shown as excluded from the jagir of Nawabag in 1866. Raje Shrinivasrao vs Raje Vinayakrao, I.L.R. , approved.

The appellant, who was the father of two respondents, filed a suit for partition and possession of certain properties. The trial court held that neither the Cutchi Memons Act, XLVI of 1920 nor the Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) applied to them as they had settled down in Madras and then in Bangalore sometime between 1928 and 1930, and as a large part of it was situate in Madras, he should prefer the Madras as against the Bombay view. The High Court dismissed the suit holding that as there was only one solitary decision of the High Court of Mysore which limited the application of Hindu Law to matters of succession and inheritance only, it had no jurisdiction to raise any such contention after the enactment of section 3 or its being applicable to them or the said properties, the said Act did not apply. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the concept of joint family does not apply to cutchi Memon; and (2) in any case there was no scope for raising any contention after enactment of the Hindu Law applicable to the Cutch, and (3) in view of the provisions contained in section Haji Aboo Bucker Sait vs The Provident Investment Co. Ltd., ; , the Bombay High Court had jurisdiction to entertain the suit. HELD : (1)(a) There was no question of having to decide whether the Bombay Act applied to cutchchi Memos and that Act did apply to Cutchi memat ers. [190 B] (b) The definition of joint Hindu family in section 3 of the , does not include Hindu Undivided Family as they are subject by custom to Hindu law of succession, including rules as to joint family property, the right of a son therein by birth and the devolution thereof by survivorship. [191 C D] (2)(a). There is no question or dispute that in matters of simple succession and succession, it was to be taken as established that these two matters among the members of the family were governed by Hindu law including the rules as regards joint family properties, its distribution according to the rule of survivorship and the right to a son in it by birth, the High court would be right in its view that the accountable persons, having been born lone before 1948, had already acquired a right by birth in the property held by their father, a right expressly saved by section 3 Of the Act. [192 E F] (3)(a), (b), (c) and (d) of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, do not make the Mahomedan Law applicable in all matters relating to Muslims nor does it abrogate the custom and usage in respect of matters other than those specified in section 2 of the Act.[192 B C] (4)(a); (b).

The appellants are manufacturers of fabrics of different types. In order to manufacture the said fabrics, yarn is obtained at an intermediate stage in the mill of the appellants and subjected to integrated process of weaving the same into fabrics. The appellants did not dispute that the different kinds of fabrics which were manufactured in the Mill are liable to payment of excise duty on their removal from the factory. They also do not dispute their liability to pay excise duty in respect of intermediate goods which have come into existence and again consumed in the integrated process for the manufacture of another commodity. The Central Board of Excise issued a circular dated September 24, 1980 purporting to interpret rules 9 and 49 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 and directed the subordinate authorities that "use of goods in manufacture of other commodity even within the place/premises specified in rule 9(1) shall be deemed to have been removed from such place or premises immediately before such consumption or utilisation". The appellants filed a writ petition before the Delhi High Court challenging the validity of the circular. During the pendency of the writ petition, the Central Government by a Notification dated October 16, 1982 amended rules 9 & 49 of Central Excise and Salt Rules 1944 with retrospective effect from June 1, 1968. By another notification issued on September 24. 1980 the Central Board directed that " use of goods produced at an intermediary stage in a factory for the purpose of production of other commodities even within that place or any premises appurtenant thereto, which may be specified by the Collector in this behalf until the excise duty leviable thereon has been paid at such place and in such manner as is prescribed in these rules or as the Collector may require, and except on presentation of an application in the proper form and on obtaining the permission of the proper officer on the form. " The appellants contended before the High Court that Rule 9(4) and rule 49 were ultra vires the provision of clause (b) of sub section (4) of section 4 of the Act inasmuch as "place of removal" as defined therein does not contemplate any deemed removal but a physical or actual removal of the goods from a factory or any other place or Premises appurtenant thereto. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) in view of section 3(1), the taxing event is the production or manufacture of the articles in question; and (ii) even assuming that there can be fictional removal as provided by rule 9, there cannot be any deemed deemed removal without the specification of the place where the excisable goods are produced. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1(i) The expression "place" is defined therein to mean a factory in such a factory and has been used for the purposes of manufacture of an end product or commodity. It must be admitted that prima facie rule 9 does not show that it also covers a case of integrated, continuous and uninterrupted process of manufacture producing a commodity at an independent stage which again is utilised in such continuous process for manufacture of a finished product. [707C D] (ii). The expression 'place of manufacture ' as defined in section 3 of the Finance Act, 1982 means not only removal from a place where goods are manufactured, but also removal within such place, or premises for captive consumption, or "home consumption" as it is called. Thus if a commodity which is manufactured in such place is taken outside the factory it will be removed and when the excisable good manufactured within the factory is removed from one plant to another it will not be a case where the goods are removed, cured or manufactured or any Premises appurtenant thereof, but any premises ancillary thereto. [807D E] (iii).

The petitioner was the holder of a permit issued under Chapter IVA of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939 to ply a stage carriage on Bulandshahr Siana Garh Bugrasi Brijghat Bhasi Babugarh Jadol Jahangirabad route in the State of Uttar Pradesh. The petitioner filed an application before the Civil Judge for staying the hearing of the suit till the disposal of a special leave petition before this Court. The Civil Judge declined to grant the request of the petitioner and fixed the suit for arguments on November 8, 1985. On appeal by the petitioner, the Additional District Judge declined the request for stay of the trial of the case till the final disposal of the Special Leave Petition before this court. The High Court dismissed the special leave petitions filed against the order of the Civil judge. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeals and setting aside the judgment of the High Court, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The jurisdiction of the State Government (the Hearing Authority under section 68 D of the Act) is exclusive in character and it is not open to a civil court to issue an order of injunction restraining the hearing authority from proceeding with the hearing or exercising its statutory functions. Whenever statute uses the expression that a decision of an authority shall be final, the jurisdiction of a civil Court to go into the correctness or otherwise of the decision is taken away. [544C D] H. C. Narayanappa and Ors. vs The State of Mysore and Ors., ; at page 753; H.C.

The appellant was convicted under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and section 161 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years and to pay a fine of Rs. 5001 or in default to undergo simple imprisonment for a further period of six months under section 161 I.P.C. The High Court maintained the conviction but reduced the sentence to one year R.I. On appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the concealment of the birth of an illegitimate child was not an offence under the Indian penal Code or any other criminal statute and if the appellant had obtained a gratification for doing or forbearing to do any official act or for showing or forbidding to show in the exercise of his official functions, favour or disfavour to any per son. HELD : (i) The order of sanction was bad in law as all the relevant papers and materials were not placed before the D.I.,G. Police. [186 G] Gokulchand vs The King, A.I .R. 1948 P.C., 82, referred to. (ii) When a public servant is charged under section 165 I. P. C. and it is alleged that the illegal grati fication was taken by him for doing, or procuring an official act, it is not necessary for the Court to consider whether or not the accused public servant was capable of doing or intended to do such an act; but if he had obtained money from Russel Nathaniel and his wife and also a gold ring from Roshan Lal, the appellant could not be said to have obtained a bribe for doing nor forbearing the official act. [185 G H] (iii) The High court was in error in holding that the appellant grossly abused his position as public servant within the meaning of section 5 (1)(d) of Prevention of Corrupt Practices Act and thereby obtained for himself a valuable thing or pecuniary advantage, and the charge under that section is established.

The appellant was convicted under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for three months and to pay a fine of Rs. 500 in default to suffer further rigorous imprisonment. The High Court confirmed his conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the sanction accorded under section 6 of the Act without which no court could take cognizance of the offences alleged against him, was not a valid sanction; (ii) the sanctioning authority had in fact applied his mind to the facts and circumstances of the case and was satisfied that in the interests of justice the appellant should be prosecuted. HELD : (i)(a) The sanction given by the police under section 4(2), Code of Criminal Procedure, is not a proper sanction. [1005 B] (b) There is no reason to distrust this statement of Mr. Bokil that before he accorded his sanction he went through all the relevant papers and after being satisfied that sanction should be given he accorded the sanction. It was not for Mr.Bokil to judge the truth of the allegations made against the appellant by calling for the records of the connected claim cases or other records in connection with the matter from his office. The papers which were placed before him apparently gave him the necessary material upon which he decided that it was necessary in the ends of justice to accord his sanction. He was an officer of high rank in the Railway and must have been fully aware that the responsibility of according the sanction against an official of the Railway subordinate to him lay upon him. It is inconceivable that an officer may sign a ready made sanc tion prepared by the Police. Apparently, the sanction already drafted contained all the material facts upon which the prosecution was to be launched, if at all concerning the acceptance of the bribe by the appellant on May 12, 1952. When the sanction itself and the evidence of Mr Boki were carefully scrutinised and read together there can be little doubt that the sanction granted in this case in no way conflicts with the observations of their Lordships of the Judicial Committee. [ 1005 C D] Gokulchand Dwarkadas Morarka vs The King, (1948) L.R. 75 I.A. 30, referred to.

The respondent landlord filed a suit for eviction of the appellant tenant from two different tenancies one for residential purpose and the other for non residential purpose. The tenancy was admitted by the tenants there, but later on it was found that the premises were let out to his wife, Manoranjithammal, as trustee and guardian an of his three minor children, section M. Gopalakrishna (appellant) shall enjoy the rents and profits of the said property for her life time, subject to certain charges mentioned in the Deed of Settlement except in respect of his two sisters. It was also mentioned that after the life time of the settlor 's wife, his son and son living at that time shall enjoy them the properties subject to various charges as absolute owners, with right of sale, gift etc. There were further directions in case of other contingencies with which we are not concerned. The appellant tenant filed an application for eviction under section 14(1)(b) of the Madras Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1939 on the ground that the landlord had no right to evict the tenants on the grounds of demolition and reconstruction. The Rent Controller held that the requirement of the landlords bona fide and ordered eviction of tenants. On appeal by the tenant, the Appellate Authority allowed the appeals filed by the appellant and set aside the orders of eviction. The High Court agreed with the view of the appellate authority that the respondent landlord had only a life interest in the premises and that it was inherent in such a life estate that it is not permissible for the landlord to invoke section 14 (1) (b). Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. A landlord has every right to demolish his property in order to build a new structure on the site with view to improve his business or to get better returns on his investment. Such a step per se cannot be characterised as mala fide on the part of the landlord. There is no merit in the contention that a single petition with regard to two different premises, though in the same premises one for nonresidential purpose and another for non residen tial purpose, is not maintainable. [275E F] M/s Raval and Co. vs K. G. 276 Ramachandra and others, ; , followed. 2.

Section 6 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950 provides that a mortgagee could enforce his right against the mortgage or after the Act came into force in respect of any part of bhumidhari rights, execution should have proceeded against trees in groves and the view taken by the executing court, that there is a distinction between trees and grove land, should have been upheld by a Division Bench of the High Court. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The position taken by both the courts below was that after the coming into force of the Act, what could still be sold in execution of the decree was the right in trees of groves as these contin ued to vest in the intermediary. This means that "grove land" and an "intermediary 's groves are equated and groves were on ly collections of trees in plots of land so as to preclude cultivation in them. The uncut trees are deemed to be parts of the "land". Section 18(1)(a) of the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition & Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1976 provides that an " Intermediary"s grove means grove land held or occupied by an intermediary as such. This meant that 'groves ' and grove land ' and an 'intermediaries ' were equated and princely collections were on the ly collection of trees, in plots, of land, so as lo preclude cultivation. The recut trees were deemed to have been parts of "land" within the meaning of section 18(i)(a). [8E F] 2. In view of this very clear legal position, it is not necessary even to consider previous definitions or to make out specious or unrealistic distinctions between standing uncut forest rights which are parts of grove and groins. The proposition is well settled, under the general law, that trees, before they are cut, form parts of 'land '. And an inseparable part is always included in the whole. In the instant case, even after that decision which, according to the aPPellant judgment debtor constitutes a complete answer to any further execution proceedings in respect thereof, the view of the executing Court that there was a distinction, between trees, and grove lands, should be upheld by the Division Bench.

The first appellant Subran was charged with an offence punishable under Section 302 I.P.C. and each one of them was convicted for an offence under Section 326/149 I. P.C., and sentenced to suffer rigorous imprisonment for three years and to pay a fine of Rs. 2000 (two thousand) and in default to undergo simple imprisonment for six months. All the accused were put on trial. The prosecution case was that all the six accused persons were armed with weapons like chopper, iron rod, knife, cycle chain etc., while the first accused Kicked him, the third accused inflicted injuries on him with a cycle chain and caused injuries on his hands, arms and legs with a chopper. The trial court convicted both the accused under Section 324 I.p.C and each of them were sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment, for one year and to suffer R.I. for six years respectively. Both the accused preferred appeals before the High Court and the conviction and sentence were set aside by the High Courts on the ground that clear evidence of eye witnesses was only against accused Nos. 2, 3 and 5 besides appellant No. 1, who had been charged with offences punishable under Sections 143, 147, 148, 341, 323, 324, 326 and 302 read with Section 149 I.Ps. The High Court acquitted two of the accused and convicted them for an alleged offence under section 326/34 I.PC. Allowing the appeal by special leave to this Court, ^ HELD: 1.1 In the trial court all the 6 accused were charge sheeted for an offenses punishable under sections 143,147, 148 and 341 read with section 149 I P.P., for causing injuries intending to cause death or such bodily injury as is sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause his death. [92F] 1.2 The intention to cause murder of Suku was not proved by the prosecution beyond reasonable doubt. There were 18 incised wounds on different parts of the body, though the deceased had also suffered stab injuries. What offence can then be said to have been committed by the four accused is that there were some other known or unknown persons who had also been a party to the commission of the crime.

The assessee, a non resident company, was entitled to royalty of five per cent on all sales effected by the Indian Company. This amount of 5% less the Indian tax had to be remitted to the assessee in the Sterling currency. For the assessment years 1967 68 and 1968 69, the assessee claimed that it was maintaining its accounts on mercantile basis alone and accordingly brought to tax the royalty amount disclosed. The Income Tax Officer completed the assessment for the first two assessment years on the basis of the returns filed by the assessee under section 10 of the 1922 Act, but did not accept the assessee 's plea that it could be said to have received the royalty amounts only when it received the same in U.K., in the shape of pounds and makes an entry to that effect in its own books at Coventry. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed the appeals holding that the assessment orders for the past years relating to the appellant reveal that the method of accounting was mercantile, that for the A.Y. 1967 68, the asses see did never contest its liability to be taxed on the amounts disclosed and further that it had committed a mistake in filing the returns for the assessment year 1969 70 on correct basis showing that the manner of accounting adopted by the appellant must be examined afresh and for that purpose allowed the appeals and remanded the matters to the Income Tax officer. On a reference made at the instance of the Revenue, the High Court answered the question in favour of the revenue and against the assessee.

The appellant was convicted for an offence under section 302 I.P.C., and sentenced to death but on appeal his sentence was reduced to one of imprisonment for life. The High Court on appeal found corroboration in material particulars, from the evidence of the approver, that he had a suspicion that the deceased had a liaison with his wife. Held, that the conviction of an accused on the testimony of an accomplice could not be sustained. It is well settled that under section 133 Cr. P.C. a conviction based merely on the uncorroborated testimony of the accomplice may not be illegal, the courts nevertheless cannot lose sight of the rule of prudence and practice which in the words of Martin B in Res. vs Boyes (I.L.R. 76 I.A. Mad. 308) is to be found in illustration (b) to section 114 of the Evidence Act which is as follows : "The court may presume that an accomplice is unworthy of credit unless he is corroborated in material details". The law being that there should be corroboration of the evidence in material particular and qua each accused, it must be the courts will, as a matter of practice, not accept the evidence Of such a witness without corroboration. Bhuboni Sahu vs King (A.I.R Mad. 309) referred to. Held further, that under the section a conviction founded merely on circumstantial evidence cannot be said to be illegal merely because it proceeds upon the uncordroborated evidence of an approver.

The appellant, a public servant, was charged with an offence under section 5(2) read with section 5 (1) (d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act and section 161 of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court accepted the prosecution case as true and convicted the appellant under section 161 I.P.C. and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years. On appeal, the High Court dismissed his appeal holding that the appellant could not be deemed to be a public Servant within the meaning of section 21 of the Act because he was not acting or purporting to act in pursuance of any of the provisions of that Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1 ) the appellant was performing only routine clerical duties and cannot be treated as an officer within the definition of "public servant" in section 21, cl. (12) Of the Prevention Of Corruption Act; (2) even if he was a public officer in the service or pay of a local authority or of a corporation engaged in any trade or industry which is established by a Central, Provincial or State Act or of any other law that he could be said to be an officer in pursuance Of any of these provisions of the . Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1)(a) The officers and servants of the Board are deemed to have been public servants only when acting or purported to act, in pursuance thereof. In view of Explanation 4 to section 21 I. P. C., the appellant cannot be deemed as a public servants within the mean ing of section 2 1, el. (13) Of section 21. [688 B] (b) The word "officer" in cl. 4 means some person employed to exercise, to some extent, and in certain circumstances, a delegated function of Government. He is either himself armed with some authority or representative character, or his duties are immediately auxiliary to those of some one who is so. The decision in Reg vs Ramajirao Jivbaji, ; , followed. (2)(a). In the present case, the appellant did not fall within the terms of cl. 5(1) of section 1, cl., (12), Indian Penal code and section 2 of the prevention of Corruption (Amendment) Act, 1958 because he had been appointed to some office for the State Electricity Board which falls within the language of Explanation. 4.

The appellant was convicted under r. 125(9) of the Defence of India Rules, 1962 and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months and fine of Rs. 500/ in default further rigorous imprisonment. He was also convicted for contravening rr. 4(b) and 141(2). The High Court set aside the conviction and sentence passed on him. In appeal by special leave it was contended that r. 141 (2) is ultra vires because it lays down a rule of evidence contrary to the law contained in section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Rule 141(1) is within the powers conferred by section 3 (1). The Rules must fall within the power given under section 3(1). Section 3 gives very wide powers. It does not empower the Court to forfeit the juar. In the instant case r.141 (2), which is in the nature of a rule, is beyond the powers given under s.3 (1) of Defence of the India Act. [273 G H] 2. Rule 142(2) falls within section 3 because it is essential to the scheme of the defence of India Act that rules may be inconsistent with existing legislation but by virtue of section 43, if otherwise valid, they would have effect notwithstanding that they are inconsistent with the existing legislation. Therefore, r. 140 (2). is within powers conferred on the Court under s,3 (l) of. the Defence Of India Act and the Rules must also provide for proof in judicial proceedings of the fact of publication. The rules must necessarily provide for the publication of orders made under the Rules and they must also provided for proof.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 109 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed their conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of Sia Ram that (i) in view of the fact that Sia had voluntarily accepted the risk of being identified in a parade but was denied that opportunity was an important point in his favour; and (ii) in any event the High Court erred in holding that the only inference which arises from the fact is that by so doing, she intended to facilitate the murder of Kunwar Singh. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) In order to constitute abetment, the abettor must be shown to have "intentionally" aided the commission of the crime. Mere proof that the crime charged could not have been committed without the interposition of the alleged abettor is not enough compliance with the requirements of section 107. A person may, for example, invite another casually or for a friendly purpose and that may facilitate the death of the invite. But unless the invitation was extended with intent to facilitate commission of murder, the person inviting cannot be said to have abetted the murder. It is not sufficient if an act on the part of the said abettor happens to facilitate his commission of crime. Intentional aiding and therefore active complicity is the gist of the offence of abetment under the third paragraph of section 108. Apart from the words attributed to Violet, there is nothing at all to show that she was aware of the nefarious design of Sibolet who was working as a Nurse with a doctor was friendly with SiaRam who was his compounder but that may rather explain why, if at all, she agreed to do as directed. [626C D] (2) The High court was dealing with an appeal against an order of acquittal in his favor. There are certain important considerations which lend weight to the view taken by the trial court that it was unsafe to convict Sia on the ground that he knew the accused prior to or at the time when he was supposed to have appeared for the complainant in the particular case. It cannot beap one assumption on another to give, to ViOlet 's conduct a meaning which it does not naturally bear. The words of Volet are at best in the nature, of a circumstance and they do not, without more, necessarily justify the inference that she is a party to the murderous design.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. His appeal against his conviction and sentence was dismissed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) when three of the four named accused were acquitted, the court could not convict only one of them on the basis of constructive liability; and (ii) in view of the possibility that one or more of the other accused participated jointly in the commission of the offence. HELD : The High Court was right in holding that though the charge as well as the evidence was directed against four named persons, a court could come to a definite conclusion that the said person had a prior concert with one or several other persons named or unnamed, for committing the said offence. A court cannot obviously make out a case for the prosecution which is not disclosed either in the charge or in regard to which there is no basis in the evidence. There must be some foundation in the Evidence that persons other than those named have taken part in the offence and if there is such a basis, the case will be covered by the third illustration. In support of the contention that a court, even in the first instance, can acquit 3 of the 4 accused named in the chargesheet on the ground that their identity has not been established, it would be making out a new case for, the prosecution, it is necessary to convict one of the named accused if it is satisfied that no prejudice has been caused to the accused by the defect in the charges. But in the second illustration, the Court can come to the same conclusion and convict one or some other unidentified persons acting conjointly along with one of several others charged. But such a conclu sion is really based on evidence. [686 D F] Mohan Singh vs State of Punjab, ; , referred to.

The petitioner, a dealer under the U.P. Sales Tax Act, 1961, was assessed to sales tax under section 59 of the Act and the same was allowed by the Sales Tax Authorities. The goods were weighed on 7th August, 1984. On 21st May, 1984, the Central Government issued an order under Section 132(1)(b) of the Income Tax Act. The petitioner challenged the said order before the High Court in a writ petition under Article 32 of the Constitution contending that the material change in section 15(1) being only the substitution of the words "the rate of duty" the customs authorities were not entitled to take into account the new rate of exchange at the appreciated value of currency in respect of the consignments stored in the warehouse prior to the coming into force of the Ordinance. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that it would not be possible for the petitioner to clear the goods on payment of duty on the date when the petitioner was actu ing expressed willingness to remove the goods.
