In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that in view of the language used in Section 15(i)(b), the rate of customs duty and tariff valuation, if any, applicable to any imported goods shall be the rate and valuation in force on the dates on which the goods are actually removed from the warehouse. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 The petitioner has no fundamental right as such to clear any goods imported without payment at that rate or without having the matter determined by the procedure envisaged and enjoined by the law for that determination. [626C] 1.2 In the instant case, the petitioner as such has no right to clear goods imported except in due process of law. Now in the facts of this case, such clear ance can only be made on payment Of duty as enjoined by Section 49 and importer may apply to the Assistant Collector of Customs for permission to store the imported goods in a warehouse pending their clearance and he may be permitted to do so; and section 68 provides that an importer of any warehoused goods may clear them if the import duty leviable on them has been paid. In that case, it is found that as the goods were removed from warehouse after the amending Ordinance had come into force, the customs Authorities and the Central Govern ment were right in taking the view that the rate was applicable to the imported 'goods should be determined according to the law prevalent on the day they were actually removed and could not be cleared because of the prohibitory orders of the income Tax Department under section 102 of the . [627D E] 1:3.

Held, that a son is liable even after partition for the debts of his father which are not tainted with immorality or illegality. The pious obligation imposed on the sons under the Mitakshara law would be sufficient to sustain the sale and defeat the sons ' suit in the same way and on the same grounds as in the case of execution proceedings. The liability of the sons to discharge the debts is a question of fact in each case dependent upon what was the estate put up for sale, what the court intended to sell and what the purchaser was intending to buy and what he purported to buy. Held, further, that where the pious obligation exists and partition takes place after the decree and there is merely a difference in the mode of enjoyment of the property by the sons which continues to exist in the lifetime and after the death of the father and which does not come to an end as a result of partition of the joint family property, all that results from partition is that the right of the son to make an application for the sale of the whole estate for payment of his debt not contracted for immoral or illegal purpose, is based on the pious duty imposed on him by the father to discharge his debts of the deceased. Held further, further that in execution proceedings it is not necessary to implead the sons or to bring another suit if severance of status takes place pending the execution proceedings as a consequence of partition and where the right, title and interest of a judgment debtor are set up for a sale as to what passes to the auction purchaser is a matter of fact. Held also, that the liability of a father who is a managing director and who draws a salary or remuneration incurred as a results of negligence in the discharge of his duties is not an avyavaharika debt as it cannot be termed as " repugnant to good morals ".

The Delhi Administration has to examine first all its witnesses as required by Rule 5(5)(a) of the Commissions of Inquiry (Central) Rules, 1972 framed under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and after it was asked by this Court by its order dated June 2, 1988 to reconsider the whole question relating to the order in which the witnesses had to be examined for being examined at the end of the inquiry. The Committee has observed thus: "Without going into the controversy if Rule 5 (5)(b) is an independent rule or is governed by section 8 B of the Act, it would direct that in the circumstances of the case three persons to whom notices under section 8B have been issued have to be examine at the beginning of the enquiry. The committee should have considered whether the petitioners were entitled to be treated as persons governed by Section 8B of the Prevention Of Corruption Act before asking them to get into the witness box for being cross examined. If the Committee had found that the petitioners are covered under section8 B then perhaps they would not have been asked to get in the witnessbox for being crossexamined till the end Of the inquiry as per legal advice given to them. This is not a case where the circumstances in which several incidents that had taken place were not known to anybody else. The affidavits and other material before the Committee show that there were a large number of persons who were eye witnesses to the incidents and why could give evidence before the committee. Taking into consideration all the aspects of the matter it is obvious that the Committee should not have in the circum stances of the present case directed the filing of a complaint against either of the petitioners for an offence punishable under section 178 I.P.C. In view of the aforesaid facts and circumstances of this case, the Committee would have then asked them to give evidence along with others who were similarly placed at the conclusion of the Inquiry as per law.

Section 3 of the Rajasthan Passengers and Goods Taxation Act, 1959 provides for levy of tax on passengers and goods carried by road or inland waterways. Section 4 lays down the method of payment of tax by means of stamps to be affixed to the tickets, and the second proviso thereto provides that where a motor vehicle is not registered in any place within the State, the tax shall be levied on the amount of such lump sum as appears to the prescribed authority to be fair and equitable having regard to the fare or freights payable for the entire journey. Section 5 lays down that the owner of a motor car or a motor cab shall pay to the State Government a lump sum in lieu of the tax so levied on fares or freight, as the case may be, which shall be fixed by the State Govern ment from time to time by notification in this behalf. The petitioners who were partners of a firm, challenged the validity of the Act on the grounds (1) that the tax was not laid upon "passenger and freights" within the meaning of Entry 56 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution; (2) that there was a difference between the levy of the lump sum payment without guidance; and (3) that, in any case, it could not be levied under Entry 56. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners: (1)(a) that section 3 of Rajasthan Passengers & Goods Taxation Rules, 1959 did not authorise the imposition of a lump sums payment by means Of stamps; (b) that in view of the provisions contained in sections 8 and 8 A and the notification making the lump amount payment compulsory, even though the route between two intra State point passes outside the State the Act had an extra territorial operation which was ultra vires the legislature. HELD: (i) The levy of a tax cannot be said to offend articles 301 and 304 of the Constitution. [526 B] (a) It is well settled that the word "pay" in Entry 56, List II includes not only the income of the citizen but also the value of freights attributable to the territory of another State when the route passes through such territory, even although the journey starts and ends in Rajasthan. [525 C D] (b)(i) It cannot be held that the Legislature intended to make a tax upon income and not upon passengers and passengers. The words "may accept" show that there may be vacant periods when no passengers or goods are transported but the tax is payable, is of any force, because there may have been days when the business done might result in tax in excess of the lumpsum payable. [500 E F] (ii) It was not correct to say that there could be vacant period when no passenger or goods were transported but only a scale of payments must inevitably differ on account of weight, bulk and nature of the goods transported. There is thus a clear classification made by the Constitution itself. No discrimination between operators of public motor vehicles using roads has been pointed out, and all operators are equally affected by the Act. Some manner of support for the argument was sought from section 9 of Rajasthan Motor Vehicles Taxation Act which provides that no tax shall really be levied in respect of all passengers carried or goods transported by motor vehicles within the state. No distinction can be made between operators who have to keep accounts and those who use roads which are not so good. There may be cases where there is days when a business done may result in taxation in excess, but there may also be cases in which tax has to be collected on actual fares and freight charges.

The appellant is a private limited company. The raw material for its manufacturing process was tin plates. The appellant served notice of retrenchment on 43 workmen, who were sought to be retrenched in service with continuity of service by the appellant and the workmen on their part agreed to co operate with the management in implementing certain economy measures and in increasing the productivity so as to make the undertaking economically viable. The workmen demanded a revision of wages from the amount payable to the workmen as back wages. The Labour Court, after examining the evidence led on both sides and considering various relevant circumstances, held that the reasons stated in the notice dated 1st July, 1974, Ext. E2, viz., heavy loss caused by non availability of raw material or recurrent power shedding and lack of profitability was a mere pretence or ruse to torment the workmen by depriving them of their livehood, the real reason being the annoyance of the appellant consequent upon refusal of the workmen to agree to the terms of settlement contained in the draft dated 5th April, 1974 and, therefore, the retrenchment was illegal. The High Court also awarded full back wages to the workers on its finding that the retrenchment is not bona fide and that the non availability or the raw material has resulted in substantial and grave injustice to the appellant. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the Appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The scope and ambit of Article 43A of the Constitution does not envisage this Court to be a regular court of appeal but confers a discretionary power on the Supreme Court to grant special leave to appeal, inter alia, where termination of service is found to be invalid. It would mean that the employer has taken away illegally the right to the work of the workman contrary to the relevant law or in breach of contract and simultaneously deprived deprived workman of his earnings. If the employer terminates the service illegally and the termination is motivated as in this case, viz. to resist the workman 's demand for revision of the wages, the termination may well amount to unfair labour practice. In such circumstances reinstatement being the normal rule, it should be followed by exercise of discretion keeping in view all the relevant circumstances. But the discretion must be exercised in a judicial and judicious manner. The reason for exercising discretion must he cogent and convincing and must appear on the face of the record. When it is said that something is to be done within the discretion of the authority, that something was to be performed according to the rules of reason and justice; according to law and not humor. It is not to be arbitrary, vague or fanciful but legal and regular. [571C D] 1.2 In the instant case, there is nothing on record to show whether the Managing Director has made any sacrifice; whether his salary and perks have been adversely affected; whether the managerial coterie has reduced some expenses on itself. If there is no such material on record, how do they expect the workmen, the less affording of the weaker segment of the society, to make their sacrifice, because sacrifice on their parts is denial of the very means of livelihood. [572E F] 1:3 The award shall stand modified to the effect that the retrenched workmen who are now reinstated shall be paid 75% of the back wages after deducting the amount paid to them as wages when recalled for work since the date of retrenchment and adjustment of the retrenchment compensation towards the amount found due and pay able.

The appellant was convicted by the Sessions Judge under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) a confession recorded during the investigation of a case by a second class magistrate not specially empowered in this behalf by the State Government under section 164 Cr. P.C., is inadmissible in evidence; (ii) a statement recorded during an investigation of such a case cannot be put in evidence under sections 74 and 80 of the Code, as no oral evidence in respect of that confession can also be led at the trial; and (iii) even after excluding the confession from consideration, the other material on record proves the guilt of the accused. HELD : (i)(a) It is well established that the discovery and arrest of the suspected offender is one of the essential steps in the course of an investigation (see section 164, Cr.P.C.) and the same is admissible in evidence and no oral or documentary evidence can be led to prove the guilt beyond reasonable doubt. [436 B] (b) The decision in Nazir Ahmed vs State of Delhi, ; , relied on. (c) In the present case, the confession was recorded during investigation of the case and as it was not recorded in the manner prescribed by section 164 Code of Criminal Procedure, the same was inadmissible in the evidence. [414 C] (d) The fact that the accused was taken by the rolice to the police post from the bazar cannot be accepted because there is nothing to show that the police was aware of the murder of Churi deceased before the visit of the ac cused to the house of Shri Mahajan. On the contrary, the evidence on record establishes beyond any manner of doubt that the dead body of the deceased was recovered after the accused had visited the house at about 9 30 p.m. when he was murdered there with the Khokhri and the fact that his wife was with him at the time of occurrence is hardly consistent with his innocence. [416 D E] (e) The evidence on records establishes beyond doubt that it was the accused and none else who caused injuries, to Churi, deceased as a result of which she died. So far as the sentence is concerned, it is not a fit case in which the extreme penalty need be exacted from the accused [416 G H] (f) The High Court altered the sentence into that of imprisonment for life. It was the case of the prosecution itself that the appellant suspected the fidelity of Ch.uri deceased and believed that Joginder had been born to her as a consequence of her adulterous conduct. Had it been so, the accused would have had a natural affection for the child and it is difficult to believe that he would have insisted upon Churi staying with him without the child. It is not necessary to dilate upon this aspect of the matter because in view of a decision of this Court in Nazir Ahmad 's case, it would be an unnatural construction of the section to hold that these safeguards were not thought necessary and could be ignored where the confession had been made to a magistrate of a lower class and that such a Magistrate was free to give oral evidence of the confession made to him. [411 G H; 414 A B] Nazir Ahmed 's Case, , referred to.

Section 82 of the Transfer of Property Act provides that where a property subject to a mortgage belongs to two or more persons having distinct and separate rights of ownership therein, the different shares in or parts of such property owned by such persons are, in the absence of a contract to the contrary, liable to contribute rateably to the debt secured by the mortgage. Section 43 provides that when there is a general law and a special law dealing with a particular matter, the special exclusion of the general or other relief shall be allowed under the Transfer Of Property Act. The question for determination in this appeal was whether section 43 could only refer to the main contract between the promisors on the one side and the promisee on the other. Held, that the whole law of mortgage in India including the law of contribution arising out of a transaction of mort gage, is now statutory and is embodied in the Transfer o f Property Act read with the Civil Procedure Code. The provisions of sections 91, 92, 101, 102, 103, 104, 105, 106, 107, 108, 109, 110, 112, 113, 114, 115, 116, 117, 118, 119, 120, 121, 122 and 123 of the Indian Contract Act do not deal with mortgages. Held further, that section 43 of the Specific Relief Act does not apply to a transaction inartistically worded the plaintiff has in substance asked for a mortgage decree up to a limit of Rs. 40,253 11 10 with interest against each defendant. Held also, that though the claim is inartic ipate, it is always open to a court to give a plaintiff such general or special relief as it deems just to the same extent as if it had been asked for, provided that occasions no prejudice to the other side beyond what can be compensated for in costs.

The appellant No. 1 was a Bachelor of Engineering (Mech.) from Karnataka University and secured 69.96% marks in the qualifying examination. Respondent No. 2, a Bachelor in Engineering (Civil) having secured 68.40 marks out of 50 marks obtained in the interview, filed an application before the Karnataka Administrative Tribunal challenging the Rules on the ground that the percentage of marks for viva voce as 33.3% of the total marks was excessive and in violation of the decision of this Court in Ashok Kumar Yadav & Ors. vs State of Haryana & Ors., [1988] Sup. S.C.R. 657, the Tribunal dismissed the petitions. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Rules are clearly in violation o f the decisions of this court in Ashok Yadav & ors. vs state of Haryana and Ors., J.T. On a direction given by this Court on 4th September, 1991, the record of the Selection Committee was produced before this Court at the time of hearing. From a perusal of the marks awarded to the selected candidates it is clear that a large number of candidates have been selected though they had secured much lesser marks than the appellants in case the above criteria is applied for selection. In view of the fact that appointments under the impugned Rules were made as back as in 1987 and only the present appellants had approached the Tribunal for relief, the case of other candidates cannot be considered as they never approached for redress within reasonable time. [497B C] 1.2 The Rules were clearly in contravention of the decisions taken by this court on 4.9.1991 in Ashok Singh & Ors vs State Of Haryana & ors., J .T. on 4 th September,1991 and Mohinder Sain Garg vs State, Punjab & Ors, J. T.

The appellants were charged with offences under section 302 read with section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that on the fateful day, the deceased came to his house and told him that he had seen God and if they followed him and his preachings, they too could see God. On 14th July, 1982, the appellant No. 1, who was a member of the family of the deceased, made an application to the Police Officer for recording the dying declaration of the murdered person. The Police Officer recorded the first information given by P.W. 2, the father of the appel lant No. 3, and his brother P.Ws. 5, 12, 15, 40 and 57 respectively. After investigation, a charge sheet was filed against the appellants under section 120B read with Section 120 B I.P.C. The Trial Court found that the prosecution had established by circumstantial evidence the complicity of Sadanand in the murder of the Collector. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction as also the sentence awarded by the Trial Court and confirmed by the High court. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The confession of a co accused is not substantive evidence against other co accused persons in the same trial. As this Court pointed out in Kashmira Singh vs State of Madhya Pradesh, ; , the confes sion of a Co accused is also not substantive Evidence against other accused persons at the trial but could only be used for lending reassurance if there by any other substantive evidence to be utilised or acted upon. In Hari Charan Kurmi & Anr. vs The State of Bihar, ; this Court observed that the confession of co accused person cannot be treated as substantive evidence and can be pressed into service only when the court is inclined to accept other evidence and feels the necessity of seeking for an assurance in support of its conclusion deducible from the said evidence. [408C D] 2.1 In a case involving the killing of the District Magistrate in his office, better investigation was expected and the State should have taken great care to ensure that every loophole in the investigation was plugged at the fight time in the right time in ac cordance with law. It is true as argued by Mr. Jai Narain for the State that it is difficult to support the charge of conspiracy with direct evidence in every case but if the prosecution relies upon circumstantial evidence, a clear link has to be established and the chain has to he completed, otherwise it would indeed be hazardous to accept a part of the link as a complete one and on the basis of such incomplete evidence, the allegation of conspiracy cannot be accepted. [413D E] 3.2 In the instant case, the prosecution relied upon circumstantial evidences, which if accepted, could provide some link between the two for the commis sion, of the offence. According to the prosecution, the accused was regularly visiting Sadanand at the jail. The jail records did not show that P. Ws. 5 and 12 were meeting at regular intervals by itself would not estab lish conspiracy. Prosecution sought to place reliance upon motive. Un doubtedly, Sadanand must have had grudge against the Collec tor for his detention as also for the demolition of the Ashram. As a matter of fact, that must have been the common reaction of all the ashramites including Yadav and Sadiq. Thus, this could not be a feature to supply the link for establishing conspiracy. [414E F] Kashmira singh vs State Of Madhya Pradesh ; , referred to.

The appellants were the workmen of a manufacturing concern known as Crompton Parkinson Private Limited and its main business was distribution of the products of a manufacturer known as "Cromptons" in one way or the other. The last of these companies was governed by the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950, which came into force with effect from April 1, 1959. Section 3 of the said Act provided that where any dispute between the company and its workmen is referred for adjudication to the Industrial Tribunal, they shall be referred to the Tribunal to fix wage scales on the same lines as are applicable in comparable concerns. The appellants contended before the Tribunal that the industry cum region formula which was the basis for fixing wages and dearness allowance had not been properly applied by the Tribunal and it had been carried away by the recommendations of the Tripartite Conference which suggested the need based minimum wages. The Tribunal rejected this contention and held that the usual pattern of having unskilled, semi skilled and skilled grades should be followed and the various workmen, though they should be known by their designation and not by the class in which they were being placed, should be fitted in these categories. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants: (1) that the Tribunal had gone wrong in applying the industry ' cum region test which is the basis of fixing wages; and (2) that there was a trend towards uniformity in the matter of scales of dearness allowance as between clerical and subordinate staff. HELD : (i) The Tribunal erred in putting emphasis on the region aspect of the industry and awarding dearness allowance to all the categories of employees including the factory workmen. [368 E] (ii) There is nothing in law to prevent the industrial tribunal from granting adjustments to the employees in the revised wage scales even in a case where previously paid employees are engaged in different lines of business for the work of clerical and inferior staff. The reason given by it for doing so is that dissimilar concerns may not be equal or there may be equal competition, wages should generally be fixed on the basis Of the comparable industries, namely, industries of the same kind in the same region. [369 E F] (iii) There was no justification to interfere with the order fixing the date from which the award would come into force. [370 A B] (iv) It is well settled that where scales of pay are existing from before no adjustment should be granted by giving extra increments and that case applies with full force to the facts and circumstances of each case. But in doing so, the Tribunal must when making comparisons take into account the total wage packet (i.e., basic wages fixed by it as well as dearness allowance) and then compare it with the total wages packet of comparable concerns and thus arrive at a just figure for basic wage, for each category of factory workmen is concerned. [371 C D] (v) There are no reason to disagree with the rate of dearness allowances fixed by the tribunal.

A usufructuary mortgage was executed in favour of the mortgagees for Rs. 1,100 and Rs. 200 respectively by the mortgagors on their own application. The mortgagees filed a suit against the appellants for redemption of certain mortgaged property and possession thereof free from encumbrances and for other ancillary reliefs. The trial court held that the Rajinama had not the effect of transferring the interest of the mortgagors in the mortgaged property to the mortgagees, and decreed the suit declaring that both the mortgages had been satisfied. On appeal the District Court set aside the decree holding that it was a complete relinquishment of the right of the mortgagor to relinquish his occupancy either absolutely or in favour Of a specified person. The High Court in second appeal held that under section 74 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, as Shiddappa did not purport to file, the same on behalf of Annappa nor had he any right to do so; by reason only of his being the registered occupant, the Raj in law was binding on his brother. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that under s 74 of Bombay Land revenue Code as Shmadappa did nothing more than a mere assertion of an adverse title on the part of the appellants could not affect the rights of the other occupants. HELD : (i) It is true that where there are more occupants than one in respect of the same occupancy each occupant has his own rights and the fact of registration of one of them as the registered occupants attracts the operation of the Code and confers certain rights or imposes certain obligations on the registeredoccupant as laid down in the Code but does not take away the rights or impose certain obligations. [601 B C] (ii) It was true that the principal one of such persons must enter into a written agreement to become the registered owner. This is for facilitating the purpose of the code but it does not mean that the other persons in whose favour the occupancy is relinquished cease to have any right. That their right as occupants remains is clearly recognised by the opening paragraph of the section which gives an occupant a right to relinquish the occupancy either totally or in respect Of the same occupa tion. [701 C D] (iii) The appellants did not intend to file the same, on behalf only of one person entering into a joint family and that their possession had a lawful origin. A mere assertion by the appellants cannot affect the subsisting equity of redemption of the mortgages or operate to shorten the period of limitation prescribed for a suit for redemption.

The respondent was a company incor porated under the Indian Companies Act, 1948. The respondent claimed that carbon paper not being paper falling within the ambit of Entry No. 2 of the Schedule to the said Notification, but a specialised article used for copying purposes, its turnover had to be assessed at the rate of 2 per cent prescribed for unclassi fied goods and not at the rates of 6 paise per rupee i.e. 6% prescribed in the said notification. The Sales Tax Officer held that carbon papers were not paper falling under Entry No 2 of Schedule I to the Notification but a residuary article used as a part of the typewriter, taxed the turnover of carbon paper for the period commencing from July 1, 1966 to June 30, 1966. The validity and correctness of this order in so far as it related to the levy of tax on carbon paper at 6% was challenged by the respondent by means of a writ petition before the High Court which allowed the same and quashed the levy. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that carbon Paper does not lose its character as paper even after being subjected to chemical processes and that ribbon is not an accessory but an essen tial part of a typewriter. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The mere fact that the word 'paper ' forms part of tile denomination of a specialised Article is not decisive of the question whether the article is paper as generally understood. The word ' paper ' in the common parlance or in the com printer sense means paper which is used for printing, writing or printing or for packing or for drawing on or for decorating, or cover ing the walls. Now carbon paper which was manu factured by coating the tissue paper with a thermo setting ink (made to a liquid consistency) based mainly on wax, non drying oils, pigments and dyes by means Of a suitable coat ing roller and equalising rod and then passing it through chilled rolls cannot be used for the aforesaid purposes but is used. according to 'the Randon House Dictionary of the English Language ' between two sheets of plain paper in order to reproduce on the lower sheet that which is written or typed on the upper sheet i. e., making replicas or carbon copies cannot properly be described as paper. It will be well at this stage to refer to a few deci sions which confirm our view. [842 C D] In the instant case, carbon paper is not paper as envisaged by entry 2 of Notification No. ST 3124/Xl02(4) dated 1st July 1966 issued under section 3 A of the U.P. Sales Tax Act, 1947 and that sale of stencil paper was therefore, not taxable at the point of levy of 10% prescribed for "unclassi nary goods" as used in Notification No ST 312 4/X1(4)/Xl002(5) dated 31st July, 1966 issued by the State Government under section 5(1) of the Orissa Sales Tax. Act, 1957 and that sales tax was payable on carbon papers at 6%.

The respondents were employed by the appellant as seasonal masons in the year 1946. In 1951, they were retrenched from service on the ground that they had disobeyed his orders and thereby committed misconduct under Standing Order No. L(a) of the U. P. Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950. The Labour Appellate Tribunal held that the management had no right to transfer the respondents 1 to 4 to the new factory and therefore the order dismissing them was illegal. On appeal by special leave, Held, that under the terms of his contract of service the sphere of his employment included only the head office and not the branches of the bank. In such circumstances when a person joined such a service, the Privy Council found it easy to imply a term of transfer and held that such a term had to be necessarily implied between the parties. Mary (Anamalai Plantation) Workman 's Union vs Seliparai Estate, [1956] I L.L.J. 343 referred to. It was not a condition of service of employment of the respondents either express or implied that the employer had the right to transferred them to a new concern stared by him subsequent to the date of their employment. Mary and Anamalai plantation Workers ' Union vs Ali Hasan, A.I.R. 1950 U.P. 343, referred to and distinguished. The question whether a person employed in a factory can be trans ferred to some other independent concern started by the same employer at a stage subsequent to tho date of his appointment was not raised in the present case.

The appellant company which was formed in 1965 and went into production, the same year, was exempted from the provisions of Chapter V A of the , by a notification issued under section 73 of the Employees ' State Insurance Act, 1948. The appellant company challenged its liability to pay special contribution under Chapter VA of the Act before the High Court of Gujarat under article 226 of the Constitution on the ground that the contribution payable under Chapter IV A was a fee and its levy was illegal as the Act did not contemplate the rendering of any service or the conferment of any benefit to the appellant company or its employees as quid pro quo for the payment. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the contributions payable under Ch. V A were a fee in order to attain legitimacy or not at all, and therefore, they could not be said to be their contributions though at a lesser rate. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The object of the amendment was to make an equitable distribution of contributions by all employers. It was not considered fair that only employers of these regions to which the benefit provisions were extended should alone make contributions and thereby help to set up a corporation. [1093G] 2.1 The object is to make appropriate provision for securing the right to work, to education and public assistance in cases of unemployment, old age, sickness and disablement, and in other cases of any undeserved want, to make legitimacy or otherwise, to all workers agricultural, industrial or otherwise work, a living wage, conditions of work ensuring a decent standard of life and full enjoyment of leisure and social and cultural opportunities. It is in pursuance of these Directive Principles that the State has enacted the . [1094H; 1095A B] Basant Kumar vs E. S. I. Corporation, ; , referred to. 2.2 In the instant case, the appellant Company which was incorporated in 1965 was exempted under Ch V A from the provision of Chapter IVA until the provisions were enforced in the area where the appellant 's factory was situated. However, this exemption was withdrawn with effect from May 31, 1969 by a Notification of the Government. The question of how soon a return may be expected or ought to be given must necessarily depend on the nature of the services required to be performed and benefits required to he conferred. In the present case, it is not shown that the charge was to be levied as a fee or neither it has sufficient constitutional protection. [ 1095B C] Basantkumar vs Eagle Textile Manufacturing Co., ; , applied. 2:3 If the charge is to be taxed as a fees, there is no quid pro viso for it. The payment of contribution by an employer towards the premium (what else is it ?) of an employee 's compulsory insurance under the falls directly within entries 23 and 24 of List III and it is wholly unnecessary to seek justification for it by recourse to Entry 97 of List I or Entry 47 of List Ill in any circum stances. [1195C D] 2:4 If the Charge was to he levied as fee, there was sufficient quid pro ceedings for payment. [1296E F] Basant kumar vs E/S I.T. Corporation ; and Gwalior Rayon Silk Manufacturing Co. Ltd. vs section 1.

The petitioners demand regularisation of their services claiming to be daily rated workmen for a long time in the mines of the National Mineral Development Corporation Ltd. The management has throughout denied the petition ers ' claim and alleged that they have been continued on humanitarian grounds for several years, even though there was no work for them; and as such there is no question of regularising the petitioners and giving them the pay of regular workers when in fact they are not doing any work for a longer period. Dismissing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The principle of regularisation of a daily rated workman and payment to him of the pay equal to that of a regular workman arises only when the daily rated worker is doing the same work as the regular workman and there being a vacancy available for him, he is not absorbed against it or not even paid the equal pay for the period during which the same worked is taken from him. [620C D] 2. The principles of regularisation are not the position. This petition must, therefore, fail. [625E F] 3. In view of the clear findings supported by evidence that there are no vacancies or work available in the establishment for absorption of the petitioners, the question of directing their absorption and regu larisation does not arise. The Court directed that all the 63 daily rated workers including the 54 petitioners mentioned in the Annexure R V to the writ affidavit be given the benefit of the voluntary retirement scheme framed by respondent No. 2 and they be paid the specified amounts in addition to their all other dues.

The plaintiffs filed a suit against the defendants for a declaration that they were entitled to have their share in the property which belonged to them. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the purchase by the plaintiffs was valid and extended to the entire interest in the mortgaged property and that in consequence the sale in execution of the mortgage decree obtained by the plaintiff was not binding on the defendants. On appeal, the High Court upheld the title of the plaintiffs to the half share of the property but confirmed the decree of the trial court as regards the rest. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) in view of section 3 of the Crown Grants Act, the entire complexion of the suit is changed with the result that the words of section 31 or section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure which governed the grant on which reliance was placed as leading to the conclusion that it barred the plaintiffs ' claim in the present suit except to the extent of an eight pies share which represented the interest of a co sharer which was not affected by the proceeding in the suit, and (ii) even assuming that the transaction was made out and was real and intended to pass title to Pir Baksh, the bar was not attracted to cases where the subsequent suit was by the heirs and assigns of the co sharers. HELD : (i)(a) The High Court was right in holding that section 41 or section 48 of the Civil Procedure Code governed the grants on which Reliance was placed on behalf Of the plaintiffs.

The appellant was tried under section 302 read with sections 34 and 109 of the Indian Penal Code for the murder of his brother. The prosecution case was that on a day previous to the date of occurrence there was a quarrel between the deceased and the appellant, which resulted in the death of the brother. On the night previous to that date there was an altercation between the two brothers and the deceased. The appellant was charged under section 307 read with section 34 I.P.C., for causing the murder. The trial court convicted and sentenced him to imprisonment for life. On appeal, the High Court acquitted the appellant but on a reference made by the Sessions Judge under section 374 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the conviction and sentence were confirmed by the High. In appeal to this Court it was contended that : (1) the omission in the F.I.R. did not vitiate the trial unless the accused succeeded in showing that they had been prejudiced in their defence; (2) the absence of compliance with the provisions of section 173(4), Cr. P.C. showed that the omission was not sufficient to sustain the conviction, and (3) the failure to comply with the mandatory provisions of sections 173(3) and 207A of the Criminal Procedure Code had caused a complete failure of justice. HELD : (i) The omission complained of in the instant case should not have a more severe effect than the omission to carry out the provi sions of section 162 or section 360 of the Cr.P,.C. [292 B] (ii) There is no doubt that those provisions have been introduced by the amending Act of 1955, in order to simplify the procedure in respect of inquiries leading upto a Sessions trial, and at the same time to safeguard the interests of accused persons by enabling them to have such a far reaching effect as to render the proceedings including the trial before the Court of Session wholly ineffective. [293 C] (iii) The failure to do so would necessarily result in re opening the proceedings and trials which may have been concluded long ago. [294 E F] (iv) In cases exclusively triable by a court of Sessions, it is the duty of the magistrate while holding a preliminary inquiry to satisfy himself that the documents referred to in section 173 have been furnished to the accused and if he found that the police officer concerned had not carried out his duty in that behalf, the magistrate should see to it that is done. [295 G H] (v) The mere fact that the Magistrate did record the evidence as required by sub section (4) of section 207A does not render the entire proceedings and the trial null and void; or is it only an irregularity curable with reference to the provisions contained in section 537(a), Cr., P. C. [296 G H, 296 A] Abdul Rahman vs The King Emperor, L. R. 61 I. A. 225, referred to. (vi) In a case where the trial was conducted in a manner different from that prescribed by the Code (as in N. Subramania Iyer 's Case), and the accused had been afforded an opportunity of being heard in his defence, the court may reopen the proceedings by insisting upon full compliance with those provisions of the code. But there is no warrant for the argument that the failure on the part of police officers concerned or of the Magistrate before whom the committal proceedings were brought to see that all the documents, necessary to give the accused persons all the information for the proper conduct of their defence are furnished. [297 G H; 296 A B] Abdul Rauf vs The Queen Emperor, (1947) L.R . 63 I.A.

Section 153A of the Bombay District Municipal Act, 1901 (Bom. VI of 1901) provides that no person shall be directed to arrange for the discharge of any effluent in such manner as may have been previously approved by the Government and as may be specified in the notice so that rendering saline or other chemicals in such a way as to render it unfit for any use by the public or is prejudicially affecting the fertility of the soil in the surrounding area. Section 153A(3) provides, inter alia, that if a person to whom the notice has been issued objects to it and the requisition contained therein is satisfied that a nuisance exists as well as to the direction of the Municipality, he may forthwith pass such orders as may appear to him necessary for the purpose of regulating the discharge thereof in the manner specified in such notice. The appellant filed an application under section 153A (1) of the Act before the Special Officer appointed under the Act to hold an enquiry into the matter and to submit a report to the Municipality. The Special Officer rejected the application on the ground that it was mala fide, arbitrary, capricious, capricious and without jurisdiction. On appeal, the High Court set aside the order of the Special officer and remanded the case for disposal in accordance with law. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) Section 153 A(3)(a) is a protection to the party objecting to the requisition. The provisions of section 153 A do not require that a special Officer must enquire into the entire matter where a party objects absolutely to the notice and the requisitioning contained therein. There would have been no need for the appointment of a special judicial officer not below the rank of a District Judge as a Special Officer if such officer was not required to inquire into the existence of a nuisance before a notice is issued to the person concerned. [398 D F] (ii) The purpose of section153A is to leave it to the subjective satisfaction of the municipality as to its existence, and on finding that it does exist to proceed further and to do something more, then the fact in question is not collateral but is a part of the very issue which the Municipality has to enquire into and decide. [399 F G] (iii) The Special officer had wrongly decided that he could not go into the question whether the nuisance existed his order must be set aside. [400 C D] (iv) Section 154A(1)(a), however, does not require a judicial officer of the rank below a District judge as a special officer if such an officer was also not required under the section to enquire and report only as to his manner of carrying it out and that dispute would be the subject of an enquiry by the Special Judge.

The appellant was charged with the offence under section 3 of the Railway Stores (Unlawful Possession) Act, 1955. The prosecution case against him was that he failed to offer any satisfactory explanation of his possession of the goods. On the strength of some information received on 28th July 1964 that some stolen railway property was being sent out of Lucknow through a motor transport agency, a Sub Inspector attached to the Railway Protection Force along with another Sub Inspector of Police raided the premises of the motor transport company at Lucknow and found that a large number of parts of railway machinery (railway engines) bearing railway marks were contained in 23 bags of metal scrap booked the same day by the appellant for consignment to Jullunder. The usual formality of preparing a recovery memo and sealing of goods in bags in the presence of witnesses was gone through. The Magistrate found him guilty and sentenced him to imprisonment for two years. On appeal, the High Court set aside his conviction and sentence on the ground that the articles seized were railway stores within the meaning of section 2(b) of the Act and as such the question of punishment under section 4 did not arise. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: (1) The prosecution must first adduce evidence to show that there was cause for reasonable suspicion of the stores being stolen or obtained unlawfully. It is only when the burden in respect of this is discharged by the prosecution that the onus shifts to the accused to account satisfactorily of his posses sion of the same. He may, for instance, show that he had purchased the property in open market where goods of this kind are usually sold or that he has bought them from someone bona fide in the belief that the vendor had lawfully obtained the possession thereof. Even in such a case the prosecution must prove that the article was the property of a railway administration. Evidence to the effect that the goods conformed to the railway Standards fails short of such proof. In most cases, the burden of proof in this respect may be discharged by leading evidence about the identifying marks on the goods or some peculiarity of the articles not to be found in cases of non railway goods. [188 D F] (2) The mere description of the article as new would not fulfil the requirements of section 3(2). There will have to be a evidence before the courts to prove that articles seized are Railway stores within tho meaning of Section 2 of the , and as there is no evidence before them to prove the identity of the items seized.

The respondent landlord terminated the lease by a notice under section 106 of Transfer of Property Act, but she did not carry on the business with her till date of her death. The Trial Court dismissed the suit on the ground that Smt. Anandi had no right to continue in occupation of the demised premises. On appeal, the High Court held that as the appellants had failed to carry on their business with the tenant during her life time as family business they were not enti tled to the benefit of the amended definition of 'tenant ' contained in section 3(vii)(b) of the Act. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the lease hold right is an heritable estate and on death of the tenant in September 1966, the tenancy rights devolved on the heirs under the 1956 Act and unless one or other ground or grounds specified in clauses 'a ' to 'k ' of sub section (1) of Section 13 are established. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Amending Act does not apply to the facts of the case and does not have the effect of divesting their vested rights in the lease held by the tenant. They are entitled to enjoy the tenancy right without any restrictions or hedge put by the Amendment Act. [32G] 2.1 In case of commercial premises governed by the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, the Legislature has not thought it fit in the light of the situation at Delhi to place any kind of restriction on the ordinary law of inheritance with regard to succession. It may also be borne in mind that in case of a commercial premises, the heirs of the deceased tenant not only succeed to the tenancy, but also to his tenan cy rights under the Rent Act which protects the heirs from ejectment except in accordance with the provisions of Section 2(1) (iii). [32H; 33A B] 2:2. There is no provision in the Act regulating the rights of its heirs to inherits the tenancy privileges of the tenanted commercial or business premises. The tenancy rights devolve on the heir under the ordinary laws of succession.

Section 68 of the Electricity Supply Act, 1948 provides that as far as practicable and after taking credit for any subventions from the State Government the Board shall carry on its operations so as not to incur a loss. Under section 64 of the Act, if the interests realised by the State were excluded from consideration, there would be surplus in favour of the Board. The appellant Board was willing to extend that scheme to all the workers except the Government servants who were on deputation and those to whom the Employees Provident Fund Act applies. The employees claimed that all workmen of the respondent Board should have the same and similar benefits and that therefore there should be no distinction between the Board 's Contributory Provident Fund Scheme and the scheme under the Employees ' Provident Fund. The Industrial Tribunal held that if the interest realised by State was excluded from the consideration, it would bring about serious injustice if they were deprived of their benefits under the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) It is true that in a electrical establishment capital investments are heavy in the initial stages, that the Board expected that after load development work and management expenses and after provision has been made for the payment of taxes on its income and profits the interests would have to be distributed as faras they are available in the following order namely: (a) interest on bonds not guaranteed under section 66; (b) interest thereon. These and other matters cannot be properly decided in the absence of a detailed examination of the finances of the appellant Board. That is why the Tribunal has dealt with the matter in a perfunctory way. It should be directed to dispose of the matter afresh in the light of the observations made in this judgment. [47 C D] (ii) The Tribunal had dealt with all the matters in a very perfunctory manner. The Tribunal did not look into the Act at all. Whether in view of the statutory obligations laid on ii under the various sections just now referred to in analysing the capacity of the board to bear any additional burden in the matter of provident fund or other amenities, the same considerations that applied in the case of private commercial concerns could be applied is a rather difficult question. [46 E F] (iii) The Board has made no effort at all to analyse the balance sheet of the Boards to show the actual results of its working. It had made no attempt to work out the financial implications of its order. It has not made it clear what exactly are the total wages. In Gramophone Co. vs Its Workmen, [1964] II L.L.J. 131, referred to.

The respondent wife filed an application before the Magistrate under section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 for grant of maintenance by the appellant on the ground that her husband was impotent and unable to discharge his marital obligations. The parties were married on May 27, 1978 according to Sunni Muslim rites. After the marriage the respondent lived with her husband till July 1978. On November 17, 1978 the appellant sent a registered notice to the respondent informing her that he had no physical disability and was prepared to keep her with him and discharged her from marital obligations, but she refused to live with her. The respondent filed an applica tion before the magistrate under section 127 of the Cr. P.C., 1973 for granting maintenance against the appellant. The Magistrate rejected the application on the view that the husband having been found to be impotently incapable of having sexual relations with the respondent, she could not insist upon living with her in the matrimonial obligations. On appeal, the High Court reversed the order of the magistrate and held that the wife had failed to prove by convincing evidence that her consent to live separately was not a just cause for the refusal of the wife to live in the husband 's matrimonial obligations, more particularly, under the Mahomedan Law where marriage is a sacrosanct contract and not a purely religious ceremony as in the case of Hindu law. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the High court had erred in ignoring the legal effect of the second proviso to sub section (3) of section 125 Cr. It was further submitted that the various authorities of the High Courts have overlooked the legal position of the Second Proviso to sub sec tion (3), and (ii) that (iii) the various Authorities of the Supreme Court were not justified in granting maintenance to the wife. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In order to find out whether a husband is impotency or unable to perform his marital obligation, more specifically, under Hindu law where marriage has been a sacrosanit contract and the court can pass an order for maintenance where neglect or refusal is proved, even if the husband is not impotant and unable discharge his matrimonial obligations this would amount to both legal and mental cruelty which would undoubtedly be a just ground as contemplated by the proviso. Similarly, where the wife has a reasonable apprehension arising from the conduct of the husband that she is likely to be physically harmed due to persistent demands of dowry from her husband 'and the wife would be entitled to maintenance from her in accordance with his means, this would not amount to either legal or mental cruelty. [707C D] 1.2 In the instant case, there was a clear finding by the courts below that the appellant had failed and neglected to discharge the marital obligations as required by the second Proviso to Sub section (1) of Section 125 of Cr.P.C. The High Court was also right in holding that it would be pusillanimous to ignore such a valuable safeguard which has been provided by the legislature to a neglected wife. [608D E] 1:3 In the present case, it is clear that the concept of cruelty remains the same whether it is a criminal case or a civil case.

The appellant was a Class III servant employed as a metal examiner in the Railway Carriage Workshops at Ajmer. He was charged under section 161 of the Indian Penal Code read with section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 for having accepted from one Nanak Singh currency notes of the value of Rs. 150 as illegal gratification as a motive for securing a job for one Kallu. The trial court convicted him and sentenced him to suffer rigorous imprisonment for six months and one year respectively under section 5 (1)(e) of Act II of 1947 and sentenced to suffer simple imprisonment for 6 months. On appeal, the Judicial Commissioner acquitted the appellant but on further appeal the High Court held that no case under section 420 I.P.C. was made out against him and set aside his conviction. In appeal to this Court by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) he was an officer in the service or pay of Government, performing as such a public servant within the meaning of section 21(9), Indian Penal code; and (2) the provisions of section 137 of the Railways Act excluded all railway servants from the definition of public servants except for purposes of Chapter IX of the Act. HELD : (i) The appellant was not an officer of the Government within the terms of section 2(9) of Indian Penal C.P.,C. [688 B] (ii) There was no delegation to him of any authority for coercion or interference nor was he an assistant appointed to help any one who was vested with such authority. The duties which he performed were not of an exalted character or very humble indeed. As the appellant had been convicted as a public servants under section5(1) (d) Of Act II Of 1947, his conviction and sentence imposed upon him by the Courts below were quite in order and this appeal must fail. [687 E F] (iii) The provisions of law in regard to the first question must be held to be applicable to the facts of the present case. The appellant had a class III servant and was employed as metal examiner known as Chaser in the railway Carriage Workshop. He, therefore, could not be said to have been an officer within the definition given in section 21 (9) Of the Indian penal Code.

The Respondent filed a suit in the Court of Sub Judge, Patiala for permanent injunction restraining the State and the Collector cum Deputy Excise and Taxation Commissioner from auctioning his half share in an immovable property consisting of a plot of land bearing Khewat No. 374, Khatuni NO. 511. Khasra No. 39710 19 situate in village Ghagga, with a building constructed thereon. The auction in respect of the said share of the Respondent in the said property was notified for June 14,1977. Just a day prior to the holding of the auction sale the Respondent filed an appeal to the District Judge who dismissed it with costs. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the Appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of section 60 of the Code of Civil Procedure do not apply to an attachment and sale under any of her statute made expressly applicable thereto. So far as the said Act is concerned, it contains a complete code providing for the modes and machinery for recovery of arrears of revenue. The attachment in a question was levied under the provisions of the aforesaid Act and the sale which was notified was also under the provi sions of the Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1887. [847C D] 2. Section 60 of Code of Criminal Procedure provides that a property is liable to attachment and sold in execution of a decree. The opening words of sub section (I) of section60 are "the following property is chargeable to attachment" and sale mentioned in sub section(1) of Section 60, that is, to attachment, and sale in execution thereof and the proviso to sub section.(1) Of section 60 sets out the properties which are not liable to such attachment or sale. [884D E] 3. The words "such attachment or sales" in the aforesaid proviso refer to the attachment and sell mentioned in subsection (1)of Section 60 that is to attachment & sale in recovery proceedings under the said act would be only such properties as are so exempted by the said sub section. There is no provision in the Act corresponding to cl.

The Special Deputy Collector of Land Acquisition awarded a total compensation of Rs. 20,000 to the appellant. The Special Deputy Collec tor of Land Acquisi tion awarded a sum of Rs .20,000 as compensation for the lands acquired by the Government at figures awarded by the Special Deputy collector. On appeal, the High Court held that having regard to the enhanced compensation granted by the Civil Court for the land under s.11(a) and (b), it was on such basis that the High court held that there were no two separate rights one a right to receive compensation which was an inchoate right which could not be elevated to the status of an asset or property and as such not asset or interest which could have been elevated to that status by virtue of section 11(a)(b) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (i) that the land acquisition proceedings and land references in respect of the properties passing on the death of the deceased were not part of the assessment record, inasmuch as long prior thereto they had vested in the Government; (ii) that for purposes of section 61 of the Act the land acquired must be deemed to have been part of an estate passing on his death; and (iii) that since the lands were lost to the estate of a deceased before the relevant date, namely, the date of his death, the initial right to receiving compensation had already merged in those awards and the only right which the deceased had was the right to agitate against the correctness of the awards and nothing more. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that there are no two distinct rights one as a right and property had not been correctly valued in the original assessment proceedings inasmuch as the lands had vested absolutely in the State long prior to the death. [337B] (2) It is well settled by this Court that when the original assessing authority has made his own valuation of the land on the relevant dates, he must resort to provisions of section 59 and proceed to make reassessment but such reassessment has to be done within the period of three years from the date the original assess ment under section 73 A of the Income Tax Act. [330C D] (3) The very issuance of the notice under section 59(a), which was done on a basis clearly unsustainable in law is liable to be quashed on this ground. [328D E] (4) It cannot be said that there has been escapement of assessment to duty because the lands in question could not have escaped assessment to income tax due to them and, therefore, no property had escaped assessment.

The appellant 's election to the District Central Cooperative Bank was not called in question on the ground that he had been defaulter on 31.1.1986, on the date when he was declared elected as Director of the Bank. The Deputy Registrar of Co operative Societies, Nagpur, by his order dated 7.12.1987 removed the appellant from the Committee of Directors of the bank holding that appellant was defaulter on 1.2.86, on 31st March 1986 and he became defaulter under section 73FF(1)(b) of the Maharashtra State Cooperative Land Development Bank Act, 1960. The Assistant Registrar of Cooperative Societies, Chandrapur by his Order dated 7th December, 1987 directed him to remain present on 2.2 .1987 at 11.00 A.M. in the Deputy Director 's office and thereafter he was working as the Director of Cooperation, Maharashtra State Co operative Land Development bank and also on 1st March, 1986 when he visited the Committee on 18.8.1986. The appellant 'rejected that he paid the dues on 21.10.86 on 18th August, 1986, on which date he was disqualified under section 74FF(I) of Maharashtra State co operative Societies Act, 1961 and rejected his contention that section 73F(1) did not contemplate the setting aside of an election as has been done by the impugned order. The writ petition filed by the appellant in the High Court challenging the aforesaid order was dismissed on 30th August 1990 holding that the dues calculated on 31 1 1986 did not mean that the disqualification on account of his being defaulter which continued from 18. 8.1986 to 21. 10.86 was extinguished and hence the appellant was not at all eligible to contest the election. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellant could be said to have made default on the first day of his directorship and on every subsequent day till the instalment or instalments were paid. The submission that the defalult must have been one committed after the Act came into force has also to be rejected on the same ground that immediately on the Act coming into force the appellant is a defaulter and so long that default continued he must be taken to have making default, stood disqualified and thereby ceased to be a member of the committee and his seat deemed to have fallen vacant. In this view of the matter there could not be any infirmity either in the notice or in the impugned orders of removal. The result is that this appeal fails and is dismissed. [683F G] Maharashtra State Board of Education vs Paritosh Sheth, ; at 1121, referred to. 1.3 The provisions relating to election have to be interpreted harmoniously with other provisions of the Act such as in section 78(1), which deals with disqualification for membership of committee. Sub section (2) of section 73G provides that a member who has incurred any disqualification under sub section (1) shall cease to be member of a Committee and his office shall thereupon be deemed to be vacant. Therefore, the moment the appellant after election continued to be in default, and, therefore, must be take to have been disqualified and thus ceased to he a member.

The respondent was in the service of the State of Maharashtra as Supply Inspector and he retired from service on attaining the age of superannuation on September 1, 1977. After his retirement he was served with a charge sheet on October 16, 1978 containing allegations of misconduct against him for the period he was in service. Enquiry into those charges was held and the respondent was afforded full opportunity to defend himself. On the conclusion of the enquiry the State Government issued orders on December 4, 1982 reducing the amount of pension payable to the respondent by 50 per cent permanently under Rule 188 of the Bombay Civil Services Rules. The respondent challenged the validity of the Government 's order by means of a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court of Bombay. A Division Bench of that Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the State Govt 's orders dated December 4 1982 on the ground that the State Govern ment had no authority in law to take any disciplinary proceedings against the respondent as he had already retired from serv ice. Allowing the appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The Government has power to reduce or withhold pension by taking proceedings against a Government servant even after his retirement is expressly preserved by the aforesaid Rules. [188B] 2. The validity of Rule 184 of Bombay Civil Service Conduct, Discipline and Appeal Rules is regulated by the Bombay civil Services Rules (hereinafter referred to as the Rules). Rule 189 contemplates withholding or withdrawing of a pension or any part of it if the pensioner is found guilty of grave misconduct while he was In service or after completion of his service. Grant of pension and its continuance to a Government Servant depend upon the good conduct of the government servant. Rendering satisfactory service maintaining good conduct is a necessary condition for the grant and continuance of pension. Rule 189 expressly confers power on the Government to withhold or withdraw any part thereof during the period of his serv ice provided that before any order reducing or withdrawing any part, of the pension is made by the competent authority the pensioner must be given opportunity of defence in accordance to the procedure specified in Note 1 to Rule 33 of the said Rules. In the present case the purpose of the inquiry was not to inflict any punishment; instead the proceedings were initiated for determining the respondent 's pension. The proceedings were taken in accordance with Rules 188 and 189 of the Rules. Therefore, the reduction of pension by 50% was too harsh and disproportionate to the misconduct proved against the Respondent. [189E F] 3. The State Government should have taken into consideration the fact that the respondent had retired from the service and the reduction in pension by fifty per cent would seriously affect his living. Accordingly, there is no authority to initiate any proceedings against him. In B.J.

The appellant, who was the landlord of a shop, applied to the District Magistrate under section 3(1) of the West Bengal (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, for permission to institute a suit against the respondent. The application was rejected by the Commissioner on the ground that he had no jurisdiction to consider the question about the validity or otherwise of the permission granted by him. The appellant then moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the order passed by the District Magis trate. The High Court dismissed the petition holding (i) that section 3 of the Act did not provide a self contained code for the grant of permission and all questions in relation to the grant or refusal of the said permission had to be decided by the appropriate authorities constituted under the Act; and (ii) that the provisions of sections 3(4) and 16 of the Bengal Alluvion and Diluvion Act, 1939, were not applicable to such applications. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (i ) that section 2(4), read with section 16 of Act IV of 1947, did not expressly exclude the jurisdiction of the civil courts; (ii). that the words of section 3 (4) read with s.16 were clear and unambiguous and they indicated that the jurisdiction conferred on the State Government by section 7 F was very wide; (iii) that in view of the provisions contained in sections 3 (3), 4 and 16, it must be held that the High court was in error in coming to the conclu sion that the permission given by the Commis sioner was invalid in law. HELD : (i)(a) Section 3(3) does not expressly excludes the jurisdiction under section 7 G of the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act, 1949, and it must therefore be held to have been impliedly excluded by the provisions therein contained in section 3. [560 F] (b) The High Courts were not justified in introducing a limitation pertaining to questions of jurisdiction in determining the scope of the width of the revisional power conferred on them by section 3 with reference to orders included within the provisions Of s.3(4). Therefore, there is no doubt that the relevant provisions of the , did not intend, even prior to the amendment of 1954, to limit the jurisdiction to the Commissioner only to cases where irregularity or illegality had been committed by the district Magistrate in granting or refusing, to grant permission. [561 G H] (c) The power conferred under section 6 F is very wide and as it must necessarily be correlated with questions of jurisdic tion. Therefore, the High Courts was not justified by introducing a limitations pertaining to question of jurisdiction. [562 C D] (ii)(a). Section 3 (2), read along with s, 16(4A) and section 16(3B) are clear and explicit words indicating that intention is that the civil court 's jurisdiction is intended to be excluded, appears to be inescapable.

The appellant, a member of the Punjab Public Service Commission, physically assaulted his wife Smt. Santosh Chowdhary, Chairman of the State Public Service Commis sion, physically injured and thereby committed gross misconduct. The Chief Minister of Punjab in exercise of the power conferred by Article 317(1) of the Constitution issued a notification dated 24th November, 1982 under Article 317 (1) that the President had referred for consideration of this Court the question as to whether Shri Saini should be removed from his office by the President on the ground of misbehaviour or incapacity. The appellant challenged the validity of the said notification on the grounds, inter alia, (i) that before making an inquiry into the matter referred to it under Article 318(1), the President should have obtained the opinion of a fact finding body for his prima facie satisfaction that a case was made out for obtaining a report from this Court on the question of misbehaviour; and (ii) that in a reference under article 317(2), this Court ought not to embark upon an examination of facts and that its function is limited to determining whether the person concerned is guilty of misconduct and whether the misbehaviour is of such a nature as to warrant the removal of the person from his post. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding (i ) that it was open to the President to make a reference to this Court under article 318(2) for consideration on a consideration of the affidavits only, and (iii) that it could not be said that an examination and assessment of facts is made by this Court instead of being made by a Magistrate or a Munsif. Dismissing the appeal to this court, ^ HELD: (1)(a) Article 317 provides that an inquiry has to be held by this court in accordance with the procedure prescribed in that behalf under article 145. [646C] (b) The power conferred on this Court to summon witnesses and record their evidence is limited only to the cross examination of witnesses who have filed affidavits before this Court. It is impossible to accept that the Supreme Court in one case and the Parliament in the other case of those others are entrusted with the limited powers of determining whether a witness is guilty or not. [643D] (c) The procedure which this Court should adopt in a Reference made by the Constitution under Article 316(1). [644E F] (d) It is difficult to accept the contention that the evidence should be recorded by this Constitution itself. [641A B] (e) There is no justification for reading into article 317 a provision which is not specifically incorporated in Order XXXVIII of the Supreme court Rules, 1966.

The appellants plaintiffs filed a suit against the respondent defendant for a declaration that the deity installed in the temple was a family deity of a private nature and the endowment being of a public nature, as alleged by them. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the temple and the deity were of a religious character, and therefore, had no application and the order passed by the respondent regarding the management was set aside. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decision of the Subordinate Judge and held that the endowment was of a purely private nature, and the respondent was fully entitled to pass orders for its management. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) It is well settled that the issue whether a religious endowment is a public or a private one must depend on the facts proved in each case and it is difficult to lay down any test or tests which may be of universal application. It is manifest that where the endowment is lost in antiquity or shrouded in mystery, there being no document or revenue entry to prove its origin, the task of the court becomes difficult and it has to rely merely on circumstantial evidence regarding the nature and origin of the endowment and the recitals of the document show that the control and management vests either in a large body of persons or in the members of the public and the founder does not retain any control over the management.

The appellant Bank formerly known as the Bharat Bank Ltd., agreed to finance the contracts and to advance monies to Malhotra against his bills for supplies under the contracts. The agreement provided that all powers hereby granted were and shall be irrevocable as long as any claims of the attorneys against the bills were subsisting in their own name or in our names in payment of such bills or other amounts and to receive the amount thereof and appropriate such receipts towards and in repayment of the advances made or to be made hereafter and all other monies due from us to the Attorneys in any account what soever. The appellant was authorised to sue for, recover and receive the monies due under the contract during the currency of the money decree obtained by him against his bill for supplies. On September 11, 1952, the appellant filed objections to the execution proceedings. The objections were dismissed on December 12, 1952. On December 12 1952, a suit in the court of the 1st Additional District Judge, Jabalpur, against Malhotra and Takhatmal was decreed in favour of the appellant. The High Court allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the power of attorney dated July 13, 1946 coupled with the endorsement on the bill dated July 19, 1948 was a clear engagement by Malhotra to pay the appellant Bank out of the monies receivable under the bill and amounted to an equitable assignment of the funds by way of security. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The power of Attorney coupled with endorsement on bills dated July19, 1948 is a revocable mandate. It gives the payee no interest in the fund. An assignment creates an interest in it and is not revocable. Read in the light of the power conferred by section 130(3) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, it is necessary to bear in mind that there was an agreement between the lender and the borrower that the debt owing to the lender would be paid out of a specific fund of the borrower in the hands of the Government authorities. The power to attorney coupled with its endorsement on bill dated June 19,1948 was a rev irrevocable mandate. [777 E F] Palmer vs Carey, ; , referred to. (2) There can be a valid equitable assignment under section 130 of the Act. Where a document does not amount to a transfer within section 130 it may apart from and independently of the section operate as an equitable assign of the actionable claim. In the present case the power was revocable because the endorsement in the bill on the Bill dated July, 19, 1949 created an interest. The endorsement on a bill dated August 7, 1946, created an inter est in a specific Fund and was irrevocable. There was thus a sufficient equitable assignment to secure repayment of loans.

The respondent was the manager of a Tea Estate under the managing agency of M/s. Gillanders Arbuthnot & Co., Ltd. The said Co. had a Provident Fund scheme for its employees. But that provident fund was not a recognised one. The assessee retired during the previous year relevant to assessment year 1963 64 and received out of this provident fund an amount of Rs. 27,948/ which represented the interest on the amount of his own contribution to the fund. The Income tax Officer assessed this amount as the assessee 's income from other sources. On appeal by the respondent, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the receipt in question being profits was assessable under the residuary section 56 of the Act and the same having not been assessed as his salary, the assessment order relating to that item of receipt was not legal. On further appeal, the Tribunal came to the conclusion that the payment made by the assessee with which we are concerned is exempt from payment of tax in view of section 17(3)(ii) of the Income tax Act, 1961. The High Court answered the question in negative and in favour of the assessee. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The receipt of Rs 27948/ by the asses see in the relevant accounting year cannot be considered as salary though undoubtedly that is an income.
