Section 17(1)(iv) provides that income of every kind which is not to be excluded from the total income under the Act shall be chargeable to income tax under the head "income from other source" if it is not chargeable to Income tax under any of the heads specified in section 1.4 items 'A ' to 'E '. In defining the expression "Profits in lieu of salary", the legislature excluded from its scope of that expression any payments received by the assesses from a provident fund, his own contributions to the Fund or any interest on such contributions. From that it follows that the receipts of Rs, 27948 and gains of business or profession or capital gains are to be considered an income from the other sources" and brought to tax under section 56.

The Bihar Act, in so far as it prohibits the slaughter of cows of all ages and calves of a cow, bull or bullock, does not impose any restrictions on the exercise of the right conferred by article 19 (1) (g) of the Constitution. Section 3 of the Act provides that no person shall slaughter a cow unless he has obtained in respect of such animal a certificate from the appropriate authority that the animal is fit for slaughter. The petitioners challenged the validity of the impugned Acts on the grounds, inter alia, (i) that the provisions of the Bihar Act infringe their fundamental rights under article 19(1)(g), and (ii) that they infringed their fundamental right to carry on their occupation, trade or business in spite of the mandatory provisions of article 19 of the constitution. Held: (i)(a) that a total ban on the slaughter can only be regulated by the State and not by any court of law; (b) that it is not possible to apply the doctrine of severability and uphold the ban on slaughter of the animals specified in the last part of article 48, and (c) that there was no total prohibition of their occupation but only some restrictions as to their age or usefulness.

The respondent was an employee of the Company in Madhya Pradesh. He had been receiving a basic salary of Rs. 245 per month. On November 28, 1955, an order of suspension was passed against him under Standing Order No. 16(1) of the Central Provinces and Berar Industrial Disputes Settlement Act, 1947. The respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court for quashing the said orders on the ground that the Standing Orders did not apply to him as he was an 'employee ' within the meaning of the Standing Order. The High Court held that the respondent was not an employee within the scope of the said Standing Order and dismissed the petition. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The Standing Orders do make a distinction between `employees ' and ` workmen ' and there may be employees who have no tickets. Standing Order Nos. 2(a), 2(b), 3(c) and 3(d) deal with a case where an employee has to have a ticket, whereas in the present case the respondent did not fulfil the necessary condition of having his name and ticket number included in the departmental Muster 's Roll. (ii) Standing Order NO. 18 does not make a difference between `employee ' and ' workmen ' as defined for the purpose of the standing Orders. (iii) Standing Orders apply to those employees only to whom tickets have been issued, but such inclusion is not an essential characteristic of an employee. Standing order No. 2 (a), therefore, must be read as enabling the Company to issue tickets to other employees only who possess tickets and whose ticket numbers are capable of being entered in departmental musters; they are not intended to exclude employees who do not possess tickets or to whom the tickets have not been issued and consequently their names only are so entered. (iv) Standing order no doubt does make a discrimination between an employee who marks his attendance and another who presents his ticket, but it is difficult to understand why two definitions of an 'workman ' in standing Order No, 2(c), should be read in their entirety and in harmony with one another. In the matter of construction of a statutory provision no question of estoppel arises and the same rule of construction should apply in the instant case.

The appellant was an undertaking owned, controlled and managed by a Government Company viz. M/s Hindustan Steel Ltd., which went into production in the year 1964 65. The workmen claimed bonus at the minimum rate prescribed under the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965, in respect of the year 1965 66 on the plea that the Alloy Steel Project was a separate establishment in respect whereof separate balance sheets and profit and loss accounts were maintained for each unit and separate profit and Loss account were maintained by the Company. The Tribunal held that alloy steel project could not be treated as separate establishments because under the Act, a company is itself an establishment which had been in existence for a long period and had been paying bonus to the employees of all such departments or undertakings. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the word "establishment" used in section 3(1) of the Act includes all different departments, undertakings and "branches of a company". Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) The Tribunal went wrong in ignoring the fact that separate balance sheet and profit & loss account were kept for each separate undertaking. No bonus was declared in respect thereof by the Labour Appellate Tribunal. [633 G] (ii) There is no provision even in the containing a prohibition to maintenance of separate balance Sheets and separate profits and loss statements for each of such units. The only exception has been in the case of workmen of the Head Office where no separate profit & Loss was worked out and the bonus was paid on the basis of the consolidated accounts. That has never been done in the present case. Therefore, there is no reason for interpreting the proviso to section 3 in the manner suggested by the Tribunal. The proviso to sub section (2) of section 16 also does not stand in the way of this claim because there is nothing to show that in any year after Alloy steel Project was set up by the existing establishments of Hindustan Steel Limited, it may not be possible to make a deduction @ 8.5 per cent of the paid up equity share capital as envisaged by section 6(d) and the Third Schedule thereto. [625 G H] (iii) There was no evidence at all that in the factory, the entire paid up capital was credited and advances were made by the Head office to the various units out of this capital or out of loans taken by the head office. In the case, there was very clear evidence that though the Company, Hindustan Steel Project is treated as an establishment newly set up for purposes of section 17(1), the exemption claimed would be fully justified.

The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 was enacted by Parliament under Article 252 of the Constitution with a view to control pollution of rivers and streams which has assumed considerable importance and urgency in recent years. The Act provides for levy of cess on water consumed by persons carrying on any specified industry and every local authority and is calculated on the basis of water consumed. Section 3 of the Cess Act provides that there shall be levied and collected a cess at such rate not exceeding the rates specified in the corre sponding Entry in column 1 thereof as the Central Government may, from time to time, by notification in the Official Gazette, specify. The cess is payable on the person carrying on the specified industry. Section 2(g) defines 'vegetable product ' as including any plant but in common parlance it is understood as refer ence to edible plants or parts of edible plants. The Cess Act was enacted with a purpose to control the pollution and to ensure that industrial effluents are not allowed to be discharged into water coarses without adequate treatment. Section 7 of the cess provides for the levy and collection of cess from the sugar manufacturers on the ground that this industry falls under item 15 of Schedule I to the Cess act. The appellant State Government issued a notification demanding water cess from its sugar factories on the grounds, inter alia, (i) that the industry fell under item No. 15 of the Schedule I; (ii) that it did not come within Entry 15 of schedule I; and (iii) that industries manufacturing sugar were covered by Entry 15 in Schedule I. The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellant. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant State that sugar manufacturing industry would fall under Item No.15 of Schedule 1. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: (1) It is a fiscal enactment, as is held by this Court in Member Secretary, Andhra Pradesh State Board for Prevention and Control Of Water Pollution vs Andhra Pradesh Rayons Ltd., [1963] Supp. 2 SCR 79. The levy and recovery of cess is on water which consumed by person carrying out the industries specified in Schedule 1 like Paper Industry and Textile Industry and even chemical industry which are covered by other entries could also be brought within Entry No. 14 of Schedule l. (2) It cannot be given the meaning of vegetables which are kept on the dining tables for dinner purposes, and it has a wider amplitude. It was further of the view that in interpreting the word 'veg etable ' one has to keep in mind the object for which the Cess is made. [532C D] (3) The cess Act is a taxing enactment. In the context in which the word "vegetables" is used in Entry 15, it cannot be said that any particular industry is brought into existence which is different from that originally existed in the sense that the thing produced is by itself a commercially different commodity whereas in the case of processing it is not necessary to produce a commer cially different article. Processing essentially effectuates a change in form, contour, physical appearance or chemical combination or otherwise by artificial or natural means and in its more complicated form involves progressive action in performing, producing or making something. [525F G] (4) The Cess is a tax levied on the consumed by a person carrying goods specified in a raw state into marketable form. It would be covered by the Act. [25H; 26A B] (5) In order to bring an industry within any of the entires in Schedule l it has to be seen what is the end product produced by that industry. Sugar cane is not a vegetable although it may be an agricultural product.

Section 10(3)(a) (iii) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960 provides that a tenant shall not be evicted whether in execution of a decree or otherwise except in accordance with the provisions of Sections 10, 12 and 13. Section 10(1) provides for the eviction of a tenant where the landlord is not occupying a non residential building in a city town or village concerned which is his own or to the possession of which he is entitled whether under the Act or otherwise (a) for the purpose of carrying on his profession as an advocate, and (b) for purposes of a business which he was carrying on on the date of the application, or (c) for a purpose of a trade in the State of Andhra Pradesh. The respondent landlord filed an application before the Rent Controller seeking eviction of the appellant tenant from the premises in question on the ground that he required the premises for the purposes of carrying out his profession and that the tenancy was not such as could be split up. The Rent Controller held that the respondent bona fide required the suit premises for carrying on the profession as a nonresidential building and dismissed the application. On appeal, the High Court set aside the order of eviction holding that the practice of the profession of an advocate was not business within the meaning of Section 10 (3) (a)(iii). Allowing the appeal to this Court, ^ HELD: 1. The expression business occurring in section 10( 3)(a)(i) is used in a wide sense so as to include the practice or profession of any person. There is no reason why a landlord who is a member of the legal or medical professions and who requires the premises to carry on his practice of his profession should be wholly debarred from obtaining possession of the premises. It is impossible to discover any reason for so making a discrimination against the liberal professions. But that would be the result if the expression 'business ' is given a narrow meaning which the appellant wants us to give to that expression.

The respondent filed a suit against the appellant for the recovery of Rs. 4,00,000 with interest and costs. The appellant contended that article 60 of the Indian Limitation Act 1908 was applicable only to suits where money was deposited under an agreement that it was payable on demand and therefore the limitation would commence from the date of payment and the suit was not barred by time. The trial court decreed the suit in favour of the respondent. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree holding that the respondent had authority to bind the appellant by a letter dated 29th September 1942 written by him to the respondent recording the agreement that he would deposit a sum of Rs 4 lacs with the appellant on demand. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that article 61 of the Limitation Act, 1908 applied only to cases where money had been deposited under a contract and not in cash and adjustment entries were made at the same time as the rest of the writing. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) A demand is something more than a mere loan of money. It will depend on the facts of each case whether the transaction is clothed with the character of a deposit of money or not. The surrounding circumstances at the time of the transaction, the pecuniary position of the appel lant are all overwhelming features to deten tion the oral as well as the documentary evidence of the respond ent that the amount was deposited with the appell ant. [578 C D] Nawab Major Sir Mohammad Akbar Khan vs Attar Singh & Ors., ; , referred to. (2) The mere fact that money in specie was not paid would not be destructive of deposit. The relationship between the parties, the surrounding circumstances and character of the amount is all overwhelming feature to concomitants the oral and documentary evidence. [579 D] (3) A banker or a promissory note would have been consistent with the case of a loan. It is precisely because of the then inability of India Supplies to repay the money immediately.

The petitioner was detained by an order of the Additional Secretary to the Government of India, Ministry of Home Affairs under section 3(1) of the , with a view to prevent him from dealing in smuggled goods otherwise than engaging in transporting or concealing or keeping smuggled goods. The grounds of detention served on the detenu showed that he had been prejudiced in making an effective representation to the Board against his detention in the absence of the summons issued under section 108 of the Customs Act to him, and that he was already in custody at the time the order of detention was served and since the detenu was already under trial, the order was liable to be quashed. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of his detention on the ground that (i) he had not been afforded an adequate opportunity of being heard; (ii) he was not given an opportunity of hearing; and (iii) there was violation of professional duty on the part of the counsel not to raise these points against the validity. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that (1) if the Court had indicated to Mr. Garg that the submission on this limited point did not find favour with the Court, he would have proceeded to argue the other points; and, (2) the detention order could only be justified against a person in detention if the detaining authority was satisfied that his release from detention was imminent and the order would be necessary for putting him back in jail. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1)(a) The fact that the detenu is in custody when the order is made does not take away the jurisdiction of the detaining author ity in making the order. What is necessary in a case of that type is to satisfy the court when detention is challenged on that ground that the detaining au thority was aware of the fact that he is already in jail and yet he was sub jectly satisfied that such an order would not detract from the order being passed for preventive detention. [849C D] (b) The mere service of the detention orders on the petitioner in jail would not take him away the jurisdic tion of the detain ing authority in making any order of preventive detention, and therefore, the provisions of section 61 of the Code of Criminal Procedure will be applicable.

The petitioners were working as casual labourers in the Posts and Telegraphs Department. They had been working for a reasonably long period on continuous basis for more than three years at the rate of 240 days per year with the Department as on 1.4.80. The grievance of the petitioners is that they are being paid wages far less than the minimum pay payable under the pay scales applicable to regular employees. The respondents contended that since the petitioners belong to the category of casual labour and were not being regularly employed, they are entitled to the same salary and allowances and other benefits as are being enjoyed by those who have been recruited regularly. Dismissing the writ petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. There is no justification for doing so. Such a classification is violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. It is also opposed to the spirit of Article 7 of the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, 1966 which exhorts all States parties to ensure fair wages and equal wages for equal work. The right to work the right to free choice of employment, the right of every one who works to just and favourable remuneration ensuring a decent living for himself and for family, the obligation to realise that if any worker remains idle on any day, the country loses the wealth that he would have produced during that day. That sense of belonging arises only when he feels that he will not be turned out of employment the next day at the whim of the management. It was for this reason it is being repeatedly observed by those, who are in charge of economic affairs of the countries in different parts of the world that as far as possible security of work should be assured to the employees so that they may contribute to the maximisation of production. [608C D] 2. The Government cannot take advantage of its dominant position, and compel any worker to work even as a casual labourer on starving wages. It may be that the casual labourers have driven him to that State. The government should be a model employer. There are several types of work such as road making, railway construction, house building, irrigation projects, communications etc. which have to be undertaken on a large scale. Development in these types of activities (even though they do not involve much foreign exchange) is not keeping pace with the needs of society. [613E F] 3. It cannot be said that the State cannot deny at least the minimum wages in the pay scale of regularly employed workmen even though the Government may not be compelled to extend all the benefits enjoyed by regularly recruited employees.[608F G] 4. There was no justification on the part of the respondents to prepare a scheme on a rational basis for absorbing as far the possible the casual labourer who had been continuously working for morethan one year in the posts and Telegraph, Department. The arrears of wages payable to the casual labour in accordance with this order shall be paid within four months from today. [508G H] 5.

Section 22(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, provides that no assessment shall be made under section 24 or section 23 to which cl. (c) of sub section (1) applies, unless a notice has been issued within the time allowed by or under sub s.(2) or sub section(3), as the case may be. Sub section (3) of section 34 provides that where a return in answer to a notice under section 22 is made whether of taxable income or not, the Income tax Officer shall, on or before the 1st day of May, in each year, give notice to the assessee requiring him to furnish within such period not being less than sixty days a return setting forth his total income and total world income during that year. Sub s.(4) of s.34 provides that if any person has no assessable income in the previous year, he shall be deemed to have been assessed to tax in pursuance of such notice under sub section.(1) or subsection (2), or having furnished a return under either of those sub sections, discovers any omission or wrong statement therein, he may furnish a return or a revised return as the ease may be within one month from the date of the service of the notice. Sub sec. (5) provides that notwithstanding anything contained in section 22(2), no assessment except to the extent mentioned in sub s. (1), shall be valid unless it is made after the expiry of four years from the end of the year in which income, profits or gains were first assessable. A return in response to a public notice issued under section 34(1)(corresponding to section 34) was served on the assessee on March 31, 1950. The Income tax officer included the sum of Rs. 59,026 in the total income of the assessee and assessed him on it for the assessment year 1945 46. On appeal by the assessee the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the notice under s.23(2) of Act was invalid as the assessee had failed to file a return within the period prescribed by section 22 (3). The Tribunal, however, rejected the contention of the appellant that since he had submitted a voluntary return on January 5, 1950, the assessment could not be completed before March 31. The High Court upheld the decision of the Appellate Tribunal and dismissed the assessee 's appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant: (i) that in view of section 22 of the Act the Income Tax Officer was precluded from issuing a notice u/s 23(2); (ii) that the return was not a true one, and (iii) that even if there had been no omission or failure on the part of the asses see to make a return of his income under s 24(1), it could not have been treated as a return for the period during which action could be taken. HELD: (1)(a) Under section 22, Income Tax Act, 1961, an assessee who has no such income need not make a voluntary statement u/S 23(1). If a return is made in response of a notice unders.22(2). there is no reason to think that a return would be treated as return u/ s 24 (1); but the return in law is not a mere scrap of paper. It is a return, such as the assesses considers, represents his true income. The contrary view is expressed by the Bombay High Court in Harakchand Makanji & Co. vs Commissioner of Income tax, ; and P.

The first petitioner is a registered Central Trade Union, claiming to represent about 85% of the officers working in various nationalised banks. The first petitioner 's representation was rejected by the Central Government on the ground that the circular dated 23.8.1982 issued by the Joint Secretary to the Government of India, Ministry of Finance, Department of Economic Affairs (Banking Division) was contrary to the mandate of the Banking Companies (Acquisi tion and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970. The petitioners contended that the Circular dated 23 8 1982 was ultra vires section 9 of the Act unless the said clause was so read as to be in harmony with the provisions contained therein. It was further contended that appointment by election is not the only mode of representative appointment but nomination is perfectly valid and more effective from the point of view of the true institutional interest, particu larly with reference to management efficiency. Dismissing the writ petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The object of the circular is to neutralise and dis criminate the Directors who will truly represent the interests of the various persons manning or dealing with the bank as an industry and a commercial enterprise. The object is to give the Board a truly representative character so as to reflect the genuine interests of all persons specified under section 9 as well as the larger and wider interest of national economy as postulated in Article 19(1)(c) and Article 43A of the Constitution. [856C D] 1.2 In a nationalised bank, everyone is as much an employee as he is an employer. There is no antithesis to the management and the employees. The distinction that traditionally existed prior to nationalisation is no longer applicable. But the legislature has left it to the Central Govern ment to specify by a scheme the manner in which the election or nomination is to be conducted, bearing in mind the true character and objective of the banking industry and its distinguishing features as a highly sensitive commercial enterprise.[857D E] 1:3. The Act does not contemplate a manage ment unmindful of the real interest of all person specified under Section 9 as also the larger interest of the national economy. It is with this object in view that the Act has envisaged a truly representa tion among workmen and artisans mentioned under sub section 3(b) of Section 9 are depositors, farmers, workers and artisanes mentioned under subsection 3(c) of section 9 are best represented by nomination, they being difficult of identification and their connection with the Bank being more remote than in the case of employees or even depositors. For these classes of people, the discretion is entirely that of the Central Gov ernment to choose the mode of representation. The Government may choose election or nominations as the appropriate mode of appointment in respect of all employees mentioned in the Act. It may be possible to appoint a representative of the depos iters by election instead of nomination. It would be perfectly in order for the Central Govt. to continue the practice followed by it prior to the circular in question or to hold election of the repre sentatives of the concerned employees and, if necessary, to amend the Scheme suitably for that purpose.

The respondent was imposed penalties under section 271(1)(c) read with section 274(2) of the Income tax Act, 1961 for concealment of particular income and furnishing inaccurate particulars. The Appellate Tribunal declined to order any stay holding that it had no power to grant such a prayer. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (i) that in the absence of any express provision in sections 254 and 255 of the Act relating to stay of recovery during the pendency of an appeal, it must be held that no such power can be exercised by the Tribunal under section 151 of the Civil Procedure Code; and (ii) that the High Court was not right in holding that the Appellate Tribunal had the power to stay the proceedings as also the collection of the penalties. HELD : (i)(a) The powers which have been conferred by section 254 on the Appellate Tribunals with widest possible amplitude must carry with them by necessary implication all such acts or employing such means, as are essentially necessary to its execution and that the statutory power carries with it the duty in proper cases to make such orders for staying proceedings as will prevent the appeal if successful from being rendered nugatory. A certain apprehension may legitimately arise in the minds of the authorities administering the Act that if the Appellate tribunals proceed to stay recovery of taxes or penalties payable by or imposed on the assessees as a matter of course the revenue will be put to great loss because of the inordinate delay in the disposal of appeals by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. [69 G H] (b) The power of stay by the appellate Tribunal is not likely to be exercised in a routine way or as a matters of course in view of the special nature of taxation and revenue. It wilt only be when a strong prima facie case is made out that the Tribunal will consider whether to stay its recovery proceedings and on what conditions and the stay will be granted in most deserving and appropriate cases where the Tribunal is satisfied that the entire purpose of the appeal will be frustrated or rendered nugatory by allowing the recovery proceedings to continue during the continuance of the appeals. [70 G H; 71 A B] (c) The Appellate Tribunals must be hold to have the power of granting stay as incidental or ancillary to its appellate jurisdiction. This is particularly so when section 220(6) deals expressly with a situation when an appeal is pending before the Appellate Tribu nal.

The respondent was appointed a constable in the U. P. Police Force and on December 1, 1945 he was promoted to the rank of Head Constable and in May 1952 he was posted as Station Officer. On September 16, 1952, the Superintendent of Police made an endorsement on his character roll that the Sub Divisional Magistrate had found substantial complaints against the integrity of the respondent, that he had also received such complaints and that his general reputation for integrity was not good, but that his transfer should be allowed to be continued in accordance with the normal procedure prescribed by sub paragraph (3) of para. 486 of the Police Regulations. The Superintendent of police made a endorsement on the report and communicated the same to the Superintendent. On December 17, 1952 the respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court for quashing the order of dismissal. The High Court held that the respondent was not covered by the first proviso to sub para (1) of cl. 486 Of the Police Regulation and as no prejudice was caused to the respondent the non compliance with the said clauses would not affect the validity of the order. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (i) that as the Superintendent had no power to dismiss a Sub Inspector, he did not have jurisdiction to proceed with a departmental trial without complying with the provisions of sub paragraph. (1), (2) and (3); (ii) that the order passed by the High court was invalid because it was substantially the same and therefore the departmental inquiry was only a further step in respect of the misconduct of the Respondent; (iii) that there was no prejudice caused to him the non observance of the said regulations would not vitiate the validity or the departmental trial. HELD : (i)(a) The High court had rightly held that it did not express its opinion on the other questions raised and argued before it. [677 D] (b) It is well settled by a long line of decisions of this Court that para. 489(2) does not apply to a case where a magisterial inquiry is ordered; but that a police officer can be departmentally tried under section 7 of the police Act after such a magical enquiry and therefore it falls within the express terms of para 486(2). The fact that in the interregnum the police received further complaints or that the C.I.D. made further enquiries does not affect its validity unless substantially the subject matter of the departmental trail is the same. In this case the departmental enquiry was held subsequent to the completion of the magisterial enquiry and, therefore it fell within the specific terms of Para. 486(1) (a).

The appellant was appointed to supertime grade II in the Super time scale of Rs. 1600 2000. He was promoted on different dates to super time grade II. The promotion of respondents 4 to 24 was challenged by the appellant in a writ petition before the High Court. A Single Judge of the High court allowed the writ petition holding that the promotion of Respondents 4 to24 was in contravention of Rule 8 of 1966 Rules and, therefore, invalid. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (i) that since the initial constitution of service was to be on and from September 9, 1966, it could only be filled in by promotion and not either by direct nomination or by transfer; (ii) that as these 28 posts were excluded from the strength of permanent posts in Specialists ' grade II, the appellant was fully qualified for being promoted to that post. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellant is entitled to be considered for the post which is deemed to have fallen vacant in September 1971 on the invalidation of promotion of respondent 7, Dr. G. section Jain, a person already holding the post in super time scale II and promoted as being found qualified for the same and for the said post to which each one of them was promoted appellant was not qualified and, consequently, he must be considered eligible for promotion from that date and that this Court should consider appellant 's eligibility for promotion when some posts were converted into a specified post. [53E F] 1.2 In view of the fact that they were selected by the Departmental Promotion Committee and the promotion was approved by the U.P.S.C., it is difficult to entertain their contention that in refusing to accept the appellant ' s eligibility for promo tion from the very date on which he refused to accept his promotion to a post for which he was not eligible, there is no justification for giving a direction that the appellant should be considered only for the purpose of promotion. [54H; 55A B] 1:3 It would not be gainsaid that whenever an unspecified specialists ' posts are converted into specified posts and assigned to a speciality it can be filled up in either by promotion or by direct recruitment as the situation warrants according to the rule and as determined by the quota rule. But it is equally possible, therefore that on a true interpretation of the 1966 Rules in general and rule 8(3) in particular it could not be gain said that whenever unspecified Specialists" posts are treated as unspecified 'specialists ' post, they can only be promoted to those posts who are eligible for being appointed to that speciality and not some one who is on top of the general seniority list in the specialists cadre.

The Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953 was enacted to bring about agrarian reforms in the State. The object of the Act was to provide for ceiling on land owned by the State and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto. Section 10A provides that where any person acquires any land by inheritance or bequest or gift which, with the lands already held by him exceed in the permissible area, than he shall furnish to the Collector a return indicating the permissible areas he desires to retain. Under section 2(3) of the Punjab Security Of Land Tenures (Amendment) Act, 1962, "small land owner" means a small holder, and has to be so prescribed. Section 19B provides that if after the commencement of the Amending Act, April 15, 1953 any person acquits or acquires any inheritance or by bequest or gifts which, in excess of the permissible limit, is comprised in surplus area at the commencement thereof, he shall within the period prescribed, furnish a declaration required by section 5 A. Section 20A provides for vesting of such lands in the Government for settlement of ejected tenants ejected or to be ejected under clause (i) of sub section (1) or section 9. Sub sections (2), (3) and (4) of section 19B provide that no person shall hold more than the permissible extent and the surplus land held by a large holder, whether acquired by voluntary transfer or gift or gift, which with the land already held, exceeds in the aggregate the permissible period of 30 standard acres. Sub section (5) provides that any surplus area will be used for re settlement of tenants ejected under cl. (i), sub section(1) and section 9B or other purpose notified by Government. The appellant 's father, who owned about 30 ordinary acres of land, was in possession and was in actual enjoyment as provided by the Act. On February 11, 1959, he inherited some of his lands from his mother in 1951. He filed a suit for permanent injunction restraining the respondents from interfering with the surplus lands. The trial court decreed the suit holding that section 19 B read with section 10A did not affect the petitioner 's rights and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant (i). that the land inherited by him and later transferred to his sons and wife were not hit by section 10 A, and (ii) that section 20A was violative of article 19(1)(c) of Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of the East Punjab Securityof Land Tenures Rules, 1953, which brought in certain significant restrictions on alienations and acquisitions of large land holders starts off in the statement of objects thus: "Some of the recent judicial interpretation that the rule of law must run close to the rule as to how the surplus area is to be dealt with in clause (a) of Section 10 A or for such other purposes, the State Government may by notification direct that the excess area shall be made available for the resettlement of tenants eject or to become ejected under el.

The plaintiffs claimed that the property in suit originally belonged to Gangashah who was the eldest among the five sons of Gangasahah. The defendants claimed that he was entitled to receive compensation in respect of the Malguzari lands and the decision of the Compensation Officer did not operate as res judicata against the plaintiff because no suit challenging the deci sion was instituted within two months from the date thereof and the plaintiffs were on that account not entitled to claim any compensation. The trial court held that the defendants had failed to establish their title to the property and decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiffs. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the decree passed by the Trial Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants: (1) that under the terms of the Chanda Patent the Zamindari devolves on the death of the holder on the male relative who is the senior most in age and not on the eldest member in the senior line, and (2) that the suit was barred by the decision given by the Compensation officer. HELD : (i) The High Court was in error in not reducing the amount of mesne profits awarded to the plaintiffs as they were entitled to raise the question only regarding the proprietary right in the property divested under section 3 of the Act. Section 14 of Act 1 of 1951 does not invest the compensation Officer with jurisdiction to determine competing claims, of persons claiming proprietary rights to the land vesting in the Government by the operation of section 3 Of the Act; (ii) that section 14 is intended to determine only the proprietary rights in the land, qua the State and is not concerned with determination of any question relating to a private dispute between two or more persons who make competing claims in the matter of compensation, relying upon their respective titles. A question regarding the person claiming proprietary right may in ordinary course be raised only in a claim against the State, and if that claim be decided against the claim, the order becomes final and conclusive; (iii) that it is not intended by an Order under section 14 to determine complicated questions of title by the adjudication of a revenue officer in a summary inquiry without even a right of appeal and to make his adjudication conclusive unless a suit be filed within two years from the time of the order. That is also clear from the terms Of section 35(7) of Act I of 1951 which provides "The payment of compensation under this Act to the creditors of a proprietor or to the proprietor in accordance with the prescribed manner shall be a full discharge of the State Government from all liability to pay compensation for the divesting of proprietary rights, but shall not prejudice any rights in respect Of the said rights to which any other person may be entitled by due process of law to enforce against the person to whom compensation has been paid as aforesaid.

Section 12(3) (a) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 provides that no suit for recovery of possession shall be instituted by a landlord against the tenant on the ground of non payment of the standard rent or permitted increases specified in the order made by the Court. Section 12(1)(b) provides that where at any stage of a suit for the recovery of rent whether with or without a claim for possession of the premises, the Court is satisfied that the tenant is withholding the rent on the grounds that the rent is excessive and standard rent should be fixed, the court may make an order directing the tenant to deposit in Court forthwith such amount as it considers proper as interim standard rent. Section 13(3)(a) provides for the passing of a decree for eviction after the expiry of one month from the date of service of notice under section 12(2). The respondent landlord filed a suit against the appellant for recovery possession of a portion of the ground floor of a building on the basis that the appellant was in arrears of rent for more than six months. The trial court decreed the suit and the appellate court confirmed the judgment of the trial Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the provisions contained in section 12 (3)(b), namely, that there is no limitation of time during which a dispute must be raised and none can be implied from the Explanation; and (2) the suit was barred by limitation. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1(a) In order to avoid the operation of section 12 of the Act the dispute in regard to standard rent must be raise before service of the notice on the tenant who has received a notice from the landlord under sub section (2), and it is not enough to raise a dispute for the first time in the written statement. [633 B C] (b) The provisions in section 11(4)(a), (b), (c) and (d) of that Act deal with orders which may be passed consequent upon dispute as to rent. It is only when an application disputing rent is made within the time contemplated by Explanation I to section 12, that the provisions in sub section(3), and (4) of section 11 are attracted.

The respondent company was a limited company incorporated in Canada. The Aluminium Ltd., a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, had a controlling interest in it as contemplated by section 2(21) of the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940. In exercise of the power given to it by article 105 of the articles of association of the respondent company, the Aluminium Ltd. appointed three permanent directors on the board of directors of the appellant company. One of these directors was Mr. L. G. Bash and the other directors had between them during the chargeable accounting periods ending on December 31, 1941, and December 31 1, 1943. In pursuance of the powers conferred by article 90 of the Articles of Association of the Respondent Company, the aluminium Ltd., appointed three temporary directors on September 31, 1939, to vote and/or from time to time to appoint a special or general proxy to vote for and on behalf of the Aluminium company in respect of the shares held by it in the respondent Company at all ordinary or extraordinary general meetings of the shareholders of the company. The question was whether in view of the said power conferred by the article, the statutory percentage should be taken at 10 per cent. per annum and not at 8 per cent per annum. Held, that on a true construction of section 2 (21) Of the Excess profits Tax Act 1940, when Mr. Gibby & Sons Ltd., had to produce the resolution of his principals authorising him to cast the votes of his principal, he could control the affairs at general meetings and as long as his authority was not revoked, as far as the company is concerned, the majority of its vote carrying shares were subject directly or indirectly to his will and ordering and, therefore, he cannot apply either of the tests mentioned above.

The respondent was serving as an Accountant, Grade II in the Electricity Department of the former State of Mysore. On 1st November, 1956 he was allotted to the new State of Karnataka with effect from 1st Nov., 1956. The post which he held came to be equated with that of I Division Clerk in the former state of Mysore, was abolished by the Indian Electricity (Supply) Act, 1948. On 30th December 1966, some persons junior to the respondent were promoted on their having passed Part I and II of the S.A.S. examination while promotion was denied to him as he had not passed the examination. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court which allowed the writ petition holding that the respondent was exempted from passing the departmental exami nation before qualifying for the promotion. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant Electricity Board that in view of the later Resolution of the Board dated 5th January 1970, it could not be thrown out on the ground of inordinate delay and laches on the part of the respondent and also on the grounds that in the circumstances of the case, the relief to the re spondent should not be denied on the plea of delay. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 The Board itself considered the ques tion in all its aspects and resolved that passing of the Resolution by the Board cannot have the effect of modifying a Regulation which was passed by the respondent in the exercise of the powers conferred by the statute. Apart from this circumstance by a subsequent resolution, the Board itself consider ed the question whether the allottees were exempted from pass ing the Departmental Examination before qualifying them for promotion to the cadre of Accounts Superintendents as before be insisted. Whatever might have been the purport of the resolution dated 19th May, 1969, the respondent by a later Resolution had resolved on insisting on the passing of examination and therefore allowed the Writ Petition. The High Court found that the later resolution did not affect the earlier Resolu tion on the point that the subsequent Resolution did not make any reference to the earlier Resolution and that there was no reference to those allottees at all. [511B C] 1.2 In any event, the plea taken by the appellant that the allottees are by impli cation exempted from complying with the requirements of passing the examination and, therefore, allowed the respondent 's claim cannot be accepted as it is incumbent on him to pass the S .A.C. examination.

The petitioner 's son was taken into police custody on 1.12.1987 by respondent No. 6, Sarat Chandra Barik, Assistant Sub Inspector of Police and Constable No.127, Chhabil Kujur, Police Station, Bishalgarh in connection with the investigation of an offence of theft and detained at the Police Outpost. At about 2 p.m., the petitioner came to know that her son had died as a result of multiple injuries inflicted on him while he was in police custody. The petitioner filed a petition under Article 32 of the Constitution praying for compensation for contravention of fundamental right to life guaranteed under Articles 21 and 22 of the Constitu tion, which was dismissed by the High Court. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1(a) It is well settled that an order for payment of compensation under Article 21 or 226 of the Consti tution is a remedy available in public law and is based on strict liability for violation of fundamental rights to which the doctrine of sovereign immunity has no application, even though it may be available as a defence in private law in an action based on tort. [605C D] (b) It follows that the decision of this Court in Kasturilal vs State of J&K and Ors., ; , is not applicable to the facts of the instant case since there was no reason to reject the finding of the District Judge that the State had failed to establish that the injuries had been caused to the deceased by lathi blows but it was asserted that the nature of injuries on the face and left temporal region could not have been caused by lathis and, therefore, the death had occurred in the manner suggested by the police in a train accident. [508D E] (c) It cannot be said that the defence of "sovereign immunity" in such cases is confined to the sphere of liability in tort, which is distinct from the State 's liability for contravention thereof and recovery of damages under private law by the ordinary process. It is an obligation of the State, to ensure that there is no infringement of the indefeasible rights of a citizen to life, except in accordance with law while the citizen is in its custody. [595F G] (d) The defence of 'solute immunity in such a case is not available to the State and in fairness to Mr. Pathak, learned counsel for the respondent State, it would be appropriate to spell out clearly the principle on which the liability of the state arises in such case. [596G H] 2(a).

The petitioner was convicted for an offence under section 302 I.P.C., and sentenced to death for an alleged offence under s.302 I. P.C. and the petitions filed by him to the President of India for commutation of the sentence were dismissed by the High Court on the ground that he had been asked for permission to interview two convicts Billa and Ranga who were under a sentence of death. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that if the Superintendent of Jail is allowed to interview the prisoners, the interviews can be permitted only subject to the rules and regulations contained in the Jail Manual. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: (1) The constitutional right to freedom of speech and expression conferred by article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution which includes the freedom of the press, is not an absolute right, nor indeed does it confer any right on the Press unless in the first instance, the person sought to be interviewed is willing to be interview. [1187B C] (2) The petitioner has been asking for permission for interview the two convicts, namely, Billa, and Rangas through their applications asking for a similar permission. It does not provide that no newspapermen will be allowed. But it does not mean that they can always and without good reasons be denied the opportunity to interview a condemned prisoner. If in any given case there are weighty reasons for doing so, which we expect will always be recorded in writing, the interview may appropriately be refused. But no such consideration has been pressed upon us and therefore the petitioner should not be allowed to appear in the second instance.

The respondent mortgaged a tea garden called the "Ishanchandrapar Tea Estate" to M/s. Das Bank Ltd., on January 19, 1950. On January 20, 1950, the Bank applied for appointment of a Receiver. On August 26, 1950 the appellant filed an application before the Subordinate Judge praying for damages from the Receiver on the ground that the fire had occurred due to his negligence. The Subordinate Judge decreed the suit on May 31, 1956 but he also allowed the respondent 's application for damages to the extent of Rs. 32,525. He directed that the Receiver should pay the amount within two months failing which the amount should be recovered from the security of Rs 50,000. Civil Miscellaneous First Appeal No. 22 of 1956 filed by the Receiver against that order was dismissed for default by the Judicial Commissioner, Tripura on December 18, 1959. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Subordinate judge who tried the suit was incompetent to enforce the surety bond executed by the appellant as he was neither the successor nor the successor in office nor the assign of the District Judge; and that under section 150 of the Code of Civil Procedure, save as otherwise provided, where the business of any Court is transferred to any other court, the transferee Court has the same powers and is entitled to perform the same duties as those respectively conferred and imposed by the Code upon the transferor Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The surety bond was executed in and for the purposes of the particular proceedings which were pending before the District judge and on the transfer of the suit the entire proceedings including the bond stood validly transferred to the court of the Subordinate Judges. [359B] (2) Under section 150, the Court for the time being is seized of the proceedings. Section 150(c) of the Civil Procedure Code provides that where any person has become liable as a surety for the fulfilment of any condition imposed on any person under an order of the court in any suit or in any proceeding J consequent thereon, the decree or order may be executed against the surety to the amount which he has rendered himself personally liable, in the manner provided for the execution of decrees. By virtue of section 150(C) the Subordinate Court was entitled to exercise the same power in the matter of the enforcement of the bond as the District Judges himself. Section 145(c), however, provides that when any person had become liable under an Order of the Court in any Suit or in proceedings J consequent thereto, the order passed by the Subordinate judges shall be enforceable at the instance of the presiding officer of the High Court. Thus, by virtue of sec. 150, a successor of the district judge who was seized of a suit and who transferred it to the Subordinate Civil Judge under the Tripura (Courts) Order of 1950 is entitled "to exercise the similar powers in the matters pending before him" being the date on which the Receiver owed no obligation in relation to the tea garden. He was put in possession of the tea gardens in his capacity as a Receiver and indeed parties had made contentions from time to time as to whether the tea estate was managed by the receiver economically and efficiently. The surety bonds were executed two months after the tea Garden was damaged by the fire which destroyed over 3,000 tea saplings. On 28th February 1950 the respondent moved an application asking for damages against the Receiver and the appellant praying that execution do issue against him be recovered. The trial court decreed the same on May 30, 1956, but he allowed the respondents ' application for damage to the tune of Rs 32,5,000 upto two months, failing which, the amount was to be recovered by the respondent from the appellant.

The Sales Tax Officer levied tax under the U.P. Wheat Procurement (Levy) Order, 1959 on the aggregate of the price of wheat by the appellants and rejected the contention that the wheat supplied was not sold by them to the Controller. In appeal the Assistant Commissioner held that the turnover resulting from supplies of wheat was not taxable since there was no sale within the meaning of section 2(h) of the U .P. Sales Tax Act, 1948. The order was confirmed in revision by the Additional District Magistrate. On a reference made by the Assistant Commis sioner to the High Court under section 66(1), the High court held that (i) there was nothing on record to show that the volition of the licensed dealer and until the State Government directed otherwise, of the Controller or the authorised officer; (ii) there had been no mutual assent between the parties to the transaction; and (iii) there could be no volition in the matter. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the transactions of supply did not result in sales, and were on that account not exposed to sales tax; (2) the supplies were made pursuant to the directions issued by the Controller under cl. 10B of the Uttar Pradesh Wheat Procure (Levy). HELD : (i)(a) The High Court was right in holding that there was a contract between the assessee and the State pursuant to which the goods were sold within the definition of the word 'sale ' as defined in section 2 (h) Of the U P. Sales tax Act, 1947. [679 G] (b) There is nothing in the Levy Order which can be accused of vitiating the free consent of the parties as defined under section 15 of the Act.

Section 10 of the Gujarat Prevention of Anti Social Activities Act, 1985 provides that no law providing for preventive detention shall authorise the detention of a person for a longer period than three months unless an Advisory Board consisting of persons who are, or have been, or are qualified to be appointed as Judges of a High Court has reported before the expiration of the said period of three months that there is in its opinion sufficient cause for such detention. Section 11 provides for the constitution of an Advisory Boards and section 12 prescribes the procedure to be followed by the Advisory Board. The petitioner was convicted and sentenced under the provisions of the Act. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging his second order of detention on the ground that there has been a contravention of the constitutional protection afforded by article 22(4) of the Constitution and therefore, the appellant is entitled to be released on July 14, 1986 as no reference had been made to the Advisory board within the period contemplated by section 11. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that there had been a violation of the Constitutional protection afforded under article 22 (4) and therefore the appellant was entitled to have been set at liberty. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The procedural requirements are the only safeguards available to a detenu since the court is not expected to go behind the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority. The procedural requirement are, there fore, to be strictly complied with if any value is to be attached to the liberty of the subject and the constitution al rights guaranteed to him in that regard. If a reference to an Advisory board is to he made within three months, it is no answer to say that the reference, though not made within 3 months, was made before the hearing of the case. If the representation made by the detenu is required to be disposed of within a stipulated period, it would be not answer to saying that the representation, although not dis posed of within three month, was disposed of before the hear ings of the matter. If, the representation is required, to he disposed of, within a specified period, the detention becomes illegal notwithstanding that it is within 3 month from the date of the second order. [209C D] 1.2 In a habeas corpus proceeding, it was not a sufficient answer to state that the procedural requirements of the constitution and the statute have been complied with before the date when the earlier order was revoked and a subsequent order was made. The real question for consideration is whether a law may be made providing for successive orders for detention in a manner as to render the protection of article 22 of the Constitu tion ineffective.

The petitioner filed a civil suit for setting aside the decree passed in Special Civil Suit No. 84 of 1977 on the ground that he had torn off the award and, therefore, the respondent was compelled to rely upon a photo copy of the original award which was produced with the application. The trial Judge rejected the objection filed by the petitioner but did not file any application within the prescribed limitation of 30 days. On appeal, the High Court dismissed the civil revision application holding that there was no written agreement signed by both the parties to refer the dispute to arbitration and that the entire responsibility of solving the dispute was entrusted to him and he had taken the responsibility. In the special leave petition to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner: (1) The previous proceedings were without jurisdiction; (2) the notice was already given to the party concerned about the filing of the award, (3) the time for making an application to set aside the award had expired and no such application was made (4) the award was not remitted under section 16(5) of the Act. Dismissing the special Leave Petition, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that on this aspect the petitioner is not entitled to challenge the award. [538C] 2.1 In the light of the facts and circumstances of the case, it cannot be said that the previous proceedings had become highly technical accompanied by unending prolixity at every stage providing a legal trap to the unwary. [540D] 2:2 There was no express or implied prohibition nor any inability of the Judge concerned. In this connection, it may be useful to refer to the observations of this Court in Prasun Roy vs The Calcutta Metropolitan Development Authority and another, A.I.R. 1988 S.C. 205 where all the relevant authorities on this point have been discussed. But in the instant case, there was not such express or explicit prohibition nor anything more implied prohibition or any inability to comply with the provisions of section 9 of the Civil Procedure Code. [541E F] 2 :3 In the instant context it is clear that the conduct of the parties that there is an arbitration agreement and by signing the award it could be said, that the parties had agreed to refer their disputes in writing to the arbitration of the named arbitrator. This agreement was done twice, firstly by signing an endorsement below the award; secondly, by entering into an agreement in the form of a letter addressed to the arbitrator wherein it was stated that both of them had appointed him as an arbitrator to resolve the disputes between them and that he made an award. All these are in writing and signed by all the parties. This, in our opinion, is clear from the narration of facts and circum stances of the instant ease.

The appellant, who was the mortgagee in possession of certain lands, instituted a suit against the respondents for recovery of a sum of Rs. 59,000 on the ground that the judgment debtor having made special request to the decree holder for an amicable settlement of the said properties, the decreeholder had agreed to the same. The trial court decreed the suit holding inter alia that the appellant 's claim to exemption under proviso (ii) to sub section (1) of section 36 was merely consequential and would follow as a matter of course on full satisfaction of the decree being recorded in column 20 of the register of applications for execution of decrees relating to execution. On appeal, the High Court set aside the judgment of the trial court and restored that of the executing court. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant (i) that section 36(5) of the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885, which exempts "any decree other than a decree in a suit to which this Act applies which is not fully satisfied by the first day of January, 1939, or pending on that date and includes a proceeding in execution for any of the purposes mentioned in clauses (a) or (b), or (c) (d) of sub section(2) of Section 2(22) of that Act; and (ii). that in view of the fact that the decree in question was recorded as adjusted, it could not be reopened under Order XXI, rule 57 of the Civil Procedure Code as amended by the Calcutta High Court. HELD : (i)(a) The expression "all the rights of the mortgagee" used by their Lordships in section 36 (5) is wide enough to include all such rights as would initiate a proceeding before the court to which the Act applies and which was not fully complied with by the 1st day of Janu ary, 1939. [586C D] (b) Section 36(1) is concerned only with assignment of debts in execution of a decree but when it contains an assignment of that debt, and of all the rights, of the mortgagor, the position appears to be free from difficulty. [596E F] (c ) The expression 'all the right of the assignee ' used by them in section 2(23) is comprehensive enough to cover a charge on the original mortgage debt but when they contain an assignment, of that liability, and are not an absolute interest, it cannot be said that there was privity of estate between the landlord and the mortgagee. [606G H] (d)(i) The words and that he had not received the notice referred to in cl.(a) of subsection (1), make it plain that an assignee of a mortgage debt is within the sub section, since section 28(5), which exempts inter alia "any suit or proceeding instituted or filed on or after the 1 st day of Febru ary , 1939, and pending on the 1th January, 1938, and includes any proceedings in execution to which these Act applies. [616A B] (ii)(a).

One Venkatacharyulu was the karta of a joint family consisting of himself and his four sons. The appellant was his concubine since 1945 until his death on February 22, 1949. By two registered deeds purporting to be sale deeds dated April 15, 1946 (Exbts. A 1 and A 2), he transferred certain properties belonging to the joint family. In 1947, after the execution of exhibit A 1, and A2 's widow and sons, instituted O.S. No. 12 of 1954 against the appellant for recovery of possession of the properties alleging that the documents dated April15, 1946 were executed without consideration or for immoral purposes and were void. The trial court dis missed the suit. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the decree in O. S.No. 62/54. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the transfers were made by way of gifts and not in consideration and were therefore invalid. HELD: (i) The transfer under exhibit A I and exhibit A 2 were not hit by section 6(h) of the . [46 B] Balo vs Parbati, I.L.R. , referred to. (ii) It is common case that future illicit cohabitation was not the object or the consideration for the transfers and the two deeds though ostensibly sale deeds were in reality gift deeds. Under the Madras school of Mitakshara law by which Venkatachallulu was governed he had no power to make a gift of even his undivided interest in the coparcenary properties to his concretine for her past services. [46 C D] (iii) The transfers were without consideration and they were invalid. [47 E F] Balos vs Parbata, I,.L. R. , approved.

Section 29(2) of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908 provides that where any special or local law prescribes for any suit, appeal or application a period of limitation different from the period prescribed therefor by the First Schedule, the provisions of section 3 shall apply as if such period were prescribed therefor in that Schedule and for the purpose of determining any period of limitations prescribed for any such suit, Appeal or application by any special, local law. The appellant who was one of the respondents in the appeal filed a suit against the respondent for recovery of certain amount of money on the ground that it was due to him from the respondent. The trial court decreed the suit holding that section 29(1)(a) applied only when a special or a local law prescribed a period within which a suit could be instituted, and that therefore, the period of one year prescribed by the first part of sub section (2) would not apply. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (i) that the expression "appeal under the Code of Civil Procedure" in article 156 of the Limitation Act includes a suit, appeals or application for which no period of time is prescribed in the First schedule; and (ii) that section 12(2), as amended by the Amendment Act of 1922, did not apply to an appeal under the Limitation act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The expression "appellate court" in Article 156 is wide enough to include a suit appeal or an application under a special law which is of a type similar to that prescribed therefor under the First and Second Schedule. [166F] (2)(a). In order to exclude the time for obtaining a copy of the decree and the day on which the judgment complained of was pronounced can be excluded, it is sufficient if the procedure for filing the appeal and the powers of the court for dealing with the appeal are governed by that Code. [167G H] (b) The words "where any special" or local laws prescribes a period for an appeal and when for that particular appeal a period is prescribed, in the first schedule to the Limitation Acts, as omission to prescribe a period, cannot be equated with the prescribing of any positive period of Limitation within which the appeal should be filed. [168A B] (c) In order that an appeal may be preferred from the decision of the Election Tribunal under section 98 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, for the purposes of sub s.(2) will be deemed to be an appeal from an original decree passed by a civil court situated within the local limits of its civil jurisdiction. [169F G] (d) The second part of s.29(2)(b) is independent of the first parts and can apply only in cases where the First Part of the Act has not prescribed any period or limitation for an application to an order of the Tribunal under s 98 of that Act against an order made by a Civil Court situated within that local limits. [170G H; 171A] (e) The third part of section 29 is independent and exclusive of the second part and can be applied only where the special law prescribes a time limit of limitation for any appeal or applica tion a period which is different from that prescribed by a First Schedule. Therefore, in order to deal with the second ground given by the High Court under its earlier part of cl. (2), it must be held that by the Amending Act of 1961, a conscious departure was made by the Legislature to impose a condition for the application of sub sec tion (2).

The appellant is a person providing transport service in the District of Mathura. He challenged the validity of the order dated May 22, 1986 passed by the District Magistrate, Mathura under section 76 of the , on the ground that the power to fix any area as a bus stand was vested in the Regional Transport Authority having jurisdiction over the area and not in the district Magistrate. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that section 76(2)(r) of the Act conferred wide powers on the District Magis trate to fix places for the bus stand/halting place '. It further observed that since the impugned order did not specifically state that the bus operators could allow the passengers to get down and pick up the passengers, it could not be construed as an order fixing the area as such as a Bus stand. Aggrieved by the said decision of the High Court, the appellant has preferred this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. Section 76(1)(r ) of the provides that no person incharge of a motor bus plying for hire shall for the purpose of taking up or setting down passengers, park or stop his bus anywhere within the limits of the municipal ity except at the Municipal Bus Stand. The other bye laws provided for a levy of a fee of Re. 1 for every 8 hours or part thereof in respect of the use of the bus stands by such buses and for the issue of a permit on such payment. The respondent in that case had obtained an order from the District Transport Authority directing the appellant to stop their buses at the busstand and to get out of the buses at that bus stand. It was not disputed before this Court that the District magistrate had passed the impugned orders in question with the object of establishing a bus stands in the area in question. That appears to be so from the order passed by District Magistrate and the letter dated 10.10.1986 written by the Executive Officer of the Town Area Committee. [717E F] T.B. Ibrahim vs Regional Transport Author ity, Tanjore, ; , referred to. 2.1 The High court was in error in upholding the impugned Order passed by a District Magistrate. It is not disputed that in the instant case no order has been passed by tho Regional Transport authority, Mathura to determine the area of parking places and halting places which are not the same as bus stands which can only be notified by the Regional Trans port Authority as held by this Court in T. B. Ibrahim 's case (supra).

Section 3(1) of the Punjab Paddy (Export Control) Order, 1959 provides that no person shall export or attempt to export or abet the export of paddy except under and in accordance with a permit issued by the State Government or any officer authorised by the Central Government in this behalf. Section 7 of the states that if any person contravenes any order made under section 3(a), he shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and also be liable to fine. The appellants were charged with an offence under section 7 of 'the Act. The trial court convicted them but on appeal the Additional Sessions Judge set aside their conviction and sentence. On appeal, the High Court held that there was no attempt on the part of the appellants to commit the offence of export. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that there had been an attempt on his part to transport paddy from Lakerkotla to Delhi and so there was an attempt at committing the offence. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) There is no provision in the Act which makes a preparation to commit an offence punishable. It follows therefore that the appellants should not have been convicted under section 4 of the . [665 D] (2) The preparation consists in devising or arranging the means or measures necessary for the commission of the offence and on the other hand, an attempt to commit it. If a man buys a box of matches he cannot be convicted of attemptedarson however clearly it may be proved that he intended to set fire to a haystack at the time of the purchase. Nor can he convicted of this offence if he approaches the stack with the matches in his pocket, but if he bends down near the stacks and lights a match which he extinguishes on perceiving that he is being watched, he may be guilty of an attempt, however clearly, it may not be proved.

The Sassoons entered into an agreement with the Sassoon on 24th February, 1920, for transfer of their managing agency rights to Messrs. Agarwal and Company Ltd., and Rajputana Textile (Agencies) Ltd., a company incorporated under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, in favour of M/s. Agarwal & Company Ltd. The Sassoosons agreed to transfer their Managing Agency to M/S. Agarwal Mills Ltd. and Rajputna Textiles (Agences) Ltd. to the respective transferees with effect from the 1st December, 1943. On the termination of the agreement M/ s. Agarwal was liable to pay tax in the hands of the person who carried on the business of the managing agency and not in the name of the company to whom it was assigned. The question for determination was whether the remuneration for the broken periods prior to the transfer of the Managing Agency by M/ S. Agarwal to M could be taxed in the assessee 's hands under section 26(2) of the Indian Incometax Act, as it stood at the relevant time. Held: (i) that on the construction of a managing agency agreement between the principal and the assignee it was clear that what was assigned was an income bearing asset which carried with it a right to the entire income that fell due after the date of assignment. The mere ownership of Managing Agency cannot as a matter of law be treated as the source of income, as explained above, any term in the managing Agency Agreement between the Principal and the agent entitling only the assignee to receive the year 's remuneration and negativing to the assignor any direct recourse to his quondam principal for his share of the income, cannot have the effect of denying to the assigningor a substantial right to a share in the remuneration if otherwise he has a vested right thereto. Lakshminarayan Ram Gopal and Son Ltd. vs The Government of Hyderabad, [1955] 1 S.C.R. 869, referred to. (ii)The mere ownership does not vest in the assignee a beneficial interest to the remuneration of the year and such a right may arise by virtue of a specific or implied term as between the transferor and the transferee, either as part of the deed of transfer or independent thereof.
